text:
An immigrant rights group sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its escalating effort to screen state voter rolls for alleged noncitizens, arguing the campaign illegally threatens lawful voters just weeks before the midterms.

The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., by the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, and a California voter seeks to block the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Department of Justice (DOJ) from forcing states to run voter registration records through federal databases to identify supposed noncitizens.

At the center of the case is the Trump administration’s claim that more than 190,000 people on California’s voter rolls may be noncitizens — a figure DHS has not publicly substantiated or explained how it calculated.

The plaintiffs say the government’s database-matching campaign poses a particular danger to naturalized citizens, who may still appear as noncitizens in federal records created before they became U.S. citizens.

“Naturalized citizens, lawfully eligible to vote, now face fear and extra scrutiny of their right to vote enshrined in their very citizenship,” the complaint reads

The lawsuit marks a new front in a growing wave of litigation over the Trump administration’s efforts to use DHS databases to police state voter rolls. Unlike several earlier cases focused primarily on the administration’s overhaul of the federal SAVE citizenship-verification system, the new challenge is broader.

The plaintiffs say DHS cannot simply switch to a different federal database to continue matching voter records and pressuring states to act on the results.

The complaint says the plaintiffs do not know whether DHS used SAVE or another federal dataset to generate the 190,832 figure it sent California officials. But they argue either approach would be unlawful without congressional authorization and the privacy protections required for federal data matching.

“No statute gives Defendants authority to require states to submit voter registration information through DHS databases, let alone allow DHS to determine if voter information is up to date for the purpose of verifying citizenship of voters and voter registrants,” the lawsuit says.

The plaintiffs also accuse the administration of placing state election officials in an impossible position by publicizing large numbers of supposed noncitizen voters while withholding the underlying names and methodology.

“Functionally, local officials have been told, under the threat of criminal, civil and financial penalty, to ‘go fish,’” the complaint says.

That concern is reinforced by DHS’s own recent retreats from sweeping claims it made about voter rolls in other battleground states.

In Nevada, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin initially alleged that as many as 15,903 noncitizens were registered to vote. But DHS officials later told state officials that figure represented only “the ceiling” of possible matches and disclosed that they had identified just 185 “potential” noncitizens after further review.

Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar sharply criticized the process, telling Democracy Docket that federal officials were “not sophisticated in their efforts to determine who is eligible to vote and who’s not, and that’s dangerous.”

DHS has expressed similar uncertainty in Pennsylvania.

The department privately told Pennsylvania election officials that it did not have “high confidence” in its public claim that 14,576 noncitizens were improperly registered there, according to a letter from Republican Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt.

DHS also acknowledged it still needed to explain how it reached that number and what federal datasets it used.

Those disclosures are significant because the new lawsuit argues that large-scale database matching is especially prone to falsely flagging naturalized citizens.

A person who once identified as a noncitizen while applying for a license, benefit or other government service may remain coded that way in an older federal record even after becoming a citizen, the complaint says.

The plaintiffs allege that such errors can result in lawful voters being forced to prove their citizenship or facing cancellation of their registrations. Elibible voter may also refrain from registering or voting altogether because they fear being wrongly labeled noncitizens or subjected to investigation.

The complaint brings eight claims, including violations of the Privacy Act, Administrative Procedure Act, Elections Clause, due process and equal protection. It also argues the administration has exceeded its constitutional authority because the executive branch has no independent power to take control of state voter registration systems.

The plaintiffs are asking the court to declare unlawful and block what they call the administration’s “list matching exercise/voter purge” against California and its local election officials.

The Trump administration violated federal privacy laws and the US Constitution by using federal databases to target naturalized citizens as alleged noncitizen voters, according to a new lawsuit Wednesday from an immigrant rights group.

The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights and naturalized citizen Pedro Trujillo allege the US Department of Homeland Security is erroneously using these databases to claim that there are more than 278,000 noncitizens registered to vote nationwide, including 190,832 in California, according to their complaint in the US District Court for the District of Columbia. Chad Dunn, the director of litigation of UCLA voting rights project, which represents plaintiffs in the lawsuit, said during a news conference that the federal government must have accurate data and follow the law when it threatens local and state elected officials with criminal investigation and jail.

“What the federal government has asked California officials do is take incorrect data, chase down voters, chase down election officials who might have been involved in registering those voters, and put them under the fear of criminal prosecution,” Dunn said.

A DHS spokesperson said in a statement that its databases are a “secure and reliable way” to verify the citizenship or immigration status of people registering to vote and urged states to join its efforts and utilize the databases.

“The department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems,” the spokesperson said. “It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”

The suing immigrant rights group said it has been forced to divert significant organizational resources toward voting rights defense, with participation in naturalization ceremonies and voter registration events already declining amid what the complaint calls a government-driven atmosphere of fear.

“I do not want this federal administration to get away with their attempts at voter intimidation or even worse, creating a second class citizenship where naturalized citizens citizens are not given the rights that they have earned,” said Pedro Trujillo, the director of organizing at the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights. He is listed as an individual plaintiff in the litigation.

The news conference was held in front of a California Superior Court building in Downtown Los Angeles and broke prematurely after a protester shouted as reporters began to ask questions.

The man stood about five feet from California gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra (D), who gave his remarks while the man interrupted.

“Let me see if I can try to finish with this rude individual not wanting to stop,” Becerra said.

Becerra later told reporters he had attended the event with no security detail.

“I’m here as a counsel for the UCLA Voting Rights Project,” he said.

“It's not an accident the federal government is trying to interfere with the right to vote.

text:
LOS ANGELES -- An immigrant rights group sued the Trump administration Wednesday to block the U.S. Department of Homeland Security from using federal databases that it alleged are being used to target naturalized citizens who are eligible to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Washington on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, alleges that DHS and the U.S. Justice Department are interfering with fair elections by using inaccurate federal databases in an attempt to buttress allegations of voter fraud.

The federal government is engaging in an “attack on the freedom to vote,” Angelica Salas, the coalition’s executive director, said at a downtown Los Angeles news conference. “This is voter intimidation.”

The lawsuit — filed on behalf of the coalition by the UCLA Voting Rights Project — becomes part of a swirl of legal moves that states, including California, have taken to fend off federal actions that threaten to create confusion during the midterms.

“It's not an accident the federal government is trying to interfere with the right to vote. ... They believe they can intimidate naturalized U.S. citizens,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor who is acting as a senior adviser to the voting project.

The lawsuit alleges that the administration might be comparing voter rolls with undisclosed government databases. Those systems can include outdated information and be riddled with errors, it said, and could produce inaccurate results that disproportionately affect naturalized voters.

“Comparing government databases to try and arrive at a list of noncitizen registrants has been shown to result in erroneous data,” the lawsuit said. “Congress has never authorized such activities and in fact has ... prohibited invasion of voter privacy through government data matches in this way.”

The Trump administration has been targeting noncitizen voting to allege it could be a source of significant fraud during the midterm elections, even though actual voting by people who are not citizens is rare. He is pushing for the U.S. Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters verified as U.S. citizens, and his Justice Department has sued to force the release of detailed voter data in 30 states and the District of Columbia, though it has not yet succeeded in those cases.

Asked to respond to the lawsuit, a DHS spokesperson said in an email: “The department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems. It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”

“DHS is laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens,” the statement added.

In June, a federal judge ruled that a recently revamped version of a federal tool can no longer be used, which critics had referred to as an unlawful centralized federal database of voter information.

U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan sided with advocacy groups that argued the recent upgrades to the program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, aggregated Americans’ sensitive personal data in a way that could result in voters being wrongly purged from voter rolls.

The lawsuit said it isn’t clear if the administration used that system to generate projections about noncitizens on voting rolls in the states or if other unknown datasets were involved.

By May, the Trump administration had run millions of voter registrations through government databases to determine their eligibility, a process that critics feared could purge valid voters from the rolls before the November elections. At least 67 million registrations, primarily from Republican-controlled states, have gone through a beefed-up verification program, or SAVE, at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and tens of thousands of those have been flagged as potential noncitizens or people who have died.

Specifically, the lawsuit by the immigrant rights group asks the court to stop the administration from pursuing a review of California’s voter list and to rescind the letter sent to the state requesting voter information. It also asks the court to declare the administration’s actions unconstitutional.

Trump’s Department of Homeland Security is claiming without providing evidence that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in just four states, including 190,832 in California.

California’s secretary of state, Democrat Shirley Weber, said in response, “I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official.”

According to the lawsuit, federal officials have not disclosed evidence supporting those figures.

text:
By Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff and Kristina Cooke

WASHINGTON, Sept 2 (Reuters) - The U.S. Justice Department warned that states risk losing billions of dollars in welfare funding if they do not report all immigrants known ‌to state agencies who are in the country illegally, according to a legal opinion released on Wednesday.

In a ‌major shift that would increase pressure on states to comply with the administration's immigration crackdown, the DOJ's Office of Legal Counsel said all states ​that receive funding for two key welfare programs must report people unlawfully present in the U.S. to the Department of Homeland Security.

Previously, only the state agencies that administered the funding for those programs had to do so. Other state agencies that might know of such immigrants, including universities and departments of motor vehicles, did not.

"Failure to comply may lead to ‌serious consequences, including loss of program funding," ⁠Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock, who signed the opinion, said in a statement.

Since taking office in January 2025, President Donald Trump has carried out a sweeping crackdown on both ⁠legal and illegal immigration, including deploying immigration agents into cities around the country and increasingly partnering with state and local law enforcement and outside companies to track down immigration violators.

The administration has repeatedly sought to penalize states that have tried to limit ​their ​cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

The change could face legal challenges from ​Democratic states, which have already sued to block ‌DHS from seeing personal details of people receiving funds under one of the programs, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families.

Courts have also limited other Trump administration efforts requiring the sharing of information on immigrants with DHS, although in some cases judges allowed immigration authorities to receive certain information, such as Medicaid data.

All 50 states, the District of Columbia and many U.S. territories receive funding from the two programs, which include Supplemental Security Income. Reuters contacted eight state attorneys general, ‌who did not immediately reply to requests for comment on how ​they might respond.

Federal TANF grants exceed $16.5 billion annually, and SSI federal benefits ​exceed $60 billion annually. Immigrants without legal status are not ​eligible for either program.

In the DOJ opinion, which is not law but is binding on ‌federal agencies, Craddock said the previous rule, issued in ​1998, wrongly narrowed the scope ​of the 1996 Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act by using the word "State" to mean a specific state agency, rather than every agency in a state government.

States could have knowledge of millions of people ​without legal immigration status inside their borders — ‌at least 19 states and Washington, D.C., allow immigrants without lawful status to obtain driver's licenses, while ​many state universities also admit such students.

(Reporting by Dan Rosenzweig-Ziff in Washington, D.C. and Kristina Cooke ​in San Francisco; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Edmund Klamann)

Klein said USCIS was created as a public-facing immigration benefits agency, while criminal investigations and immigration enforcement functions were primarily assigned elsewhere within DHS.

text:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services has purchased body-worn cameras, a notable step for an agency long associated with processing immigration benefits as the Trump administration expands its investigative and enforcement powers.

Federal procurement records show USCIS awarded a $159,675 contract to Axon for body-worn cameras, related equipment, storage services and training. The delivery order, issued September 1, runs through August 31, 2027, with work taking place in Maryland.

The camera purchase comes as USCIS expands its role beyond processing immigration benefits and into law enforcement. The agency has previously said it plans to recruit and train special agents with authority to make arrests, carry firearms and execute search and arrest warrants.

Read More on News

USCIS said the agents will investigate immigration fraud, national security threats and other violations of immigration law, adding new enforcement powers to an agency traditionally focused on adjudicating applications for green cards, citizenship and other immigration benefits.

Former agency officials say the purchase is notable because USCIS has traditionally operated differently from enforcement-focused Department of Homeland Security (DHS) core components such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP).

Douglas S. Pierce, a former USCIS supervisor who retired in late 2025 after more than three decades with the Immigration and Naturalization Service and USCIS, told Newsweek the purchase is "very unusual."

"To my knowledge, USCIS has not previously purchased or used body-worn cameras for its personnel before," Pierce said.

The records do not indicate how many cameras were purchased, who will use them, or how they will be deployed.

In a statement to Newsweek Wednesday, USCIS Spokesman Zach Kahler said the agency carries out its mission "safely, professionally, and consistent with law and policy."

"The agency evaluates tools and training that help employees do their jobs effectively while supporting accountability, transparency, and public and workforce safety. Body-worn cameras support these goals in certain settings," Kahler said. "For safety and security reasons, USCIS does not discuss deployment details, equipment assignments, operational procedures, technical settings, or future procurement plans. Any use of body-worn cameras follows applicable law, privacy rules, records requirements, and agency policy.”

Changing Roles for USCIS Agents

Pierce said the equipment could be used by officers in the agency's Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate during site inspections and home visits, or by personnel involved in investigations, arrests or search-warrant operations.

USCIS is taking on authorities more commonly associated with federal law enforcement agencies.

In September 2025, USCIS announced plans to create a cadre of special agents authorized to make arrests, carry firearms and execute search and arrest warrants. The agency said the initiative would strengthen its ability to investigate immigration fraud, national security threats and other violations of immigration law.

USCIS is expanding its Homeland Defenders program, part of the agency's push into investigative and enforcement functions. USCIS has said more than 700 Homeland Defenders have already been onboarded and that recruits receive training in immigration law, national security, fraud detection and agency procedures before entering the workforce.

The agency told Newsweek Wednesday that the Homeland Defender position was unarmed and different to its special agent role.

More recently, USCIS reinstated a policy permitting neighborhood investigations as part of the naturalization process. Under guidance issued on August 25, officers may seek information outside government databases when determining whether an applicant meets the requirements for citizenship.

Adam Klein, co-founder of Globali.ai and a former senior DHS official, said the purchase would have been highly "unusual" when he was at USCIS because the agency was intentionally separated from the federal government's immigration enforcement functions when DHS was created in 2003.

"When DHS stood up on March 1, 2003, the former INS was dismantled and its missions were deliberately divided," Klein told Newsweek. "Importantly, BCIS was not given the same law-enforcement authorities that were delegated to ICE. That was not an accidental distinction."

Klein said USCIS was created as a public-facing immigration benefits agency, while criminal investigations and immigration enforcement functions were primarily assigned elsewhere within DHS.

USCIS is now led by immigration hard-liner Joseph Edlow, who was confirmed as director in July 2025 after previously serving as the agency's chief counsel, deputy director for policy and acting director during President Donald Trump's first term. Before joining USCIS leadership, Edlow worked at ICE and on immigration and border security issues for both the Justice Department and Congress.

The Trump administration has utilized USCIS to tighten legal immigration, making green cards and citizenship more expensive and difficult to obtain. The agency has increased fees across several legal pathways and proposed raising naturalization fees, while expanding background checks, neighborhood investigations and scrutiny of applicants.

Klein said the camera purchase raises questions about how far USCIS is moving from that original mission.

"More than two decades later, USCIS is adding special agents with law-enforcement authorities, recruiting 'Homeland Defenders'…and now purchasing body-worn cameras," he said.

"Taken together, however, they suggest that the institutional line drawn when DHS was created in 2003 is being redrawn."

Pierce said the timing raises questions about how the agency intends to carry out its expanding responsibilities.

"I would pay particular attention to whether USCIS officers will be the ones conducting the neighborhood investigations and examinations as outlined in the memo from August 25, or whether they bring in other agencies, such as CBP or HSI," he said.

The size of the contract suggests the purchase is unlikely to support a broad rollout across the agency, Pierce added.

"This amount of money is unlikely to pay for a large-scale equipping and training of many officers," he said. "It could very well be a pilot program, or it could signal that there will be relatively few officers issued this equipment."

The order was placed through an existing Department of Homeland Security contracting vehicle used by other agencies to acquire Axon equipment. ICE and CBP have previously used the same company for substantially larger body-camera purchases.

ICE has been expanding body-camera use nationwide. Following fatal shootings during enforcement operations in Texas and Maine in 2026, agency officials announced plans requiring at least one camera-equipped officer on arrest teams and continued a broader rollout of body-worn cameras across field offices.

The USCIS bodycam contract is relatively modest by comparison. But it comes as the agency widens its investigative and enforcement remit beyond its traditional role adjudicating immigration benefits.

Key questions remain unanswered. USCIS has not disclosed how many cameras were purchased, which offices will receive them, or whether additional acquisitions are planned. Nor has it said whether the equipment will be assigned to special agents, Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate personnel, officers conducting naturalization investigations, or another group entirely.

For now, the procurement records establish only that USCIS has acquired body-worn cameras. What role they will play in the agency's changing mission remains unclear.

"If USCIS personnel are being equipped with body cameras because they will be performing functions traditionally associated with law enforcement, then the cameras are a small part of a much larger shift: USCIS is moving away from the public-facing immigration benefits agency created in 2003 and toward something fundamentally different," Klein said.

Update 9/2/26, 12:32 p.m. ET: This article was updated with comment from USCIS.

text:
GREENBELT, Maryland - A federal judge on Sept 2 blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a new executive order limiting the number of people eligible for birthright citizenship that President Donald Trump issued after the US Supreme Court rejected his previous effort.

US District Judge Deborah Boardman in Greenbelt, Maryland, issued a preliminary injunction at the request of immigrant rights advocates who had in 2025 secured a ruling from her blocking the Trump administration from enforcing his initial 2025 executive order curtailing birthright citizenship.

The US Supreme Court on June 30 rejected that initial effort to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent ​residents, known as green card holders, finding it violated the citizenship clause of the US Constitution’s 14th Amendment.

The clause, which was the focus of the Supreme Court’s 6-3 ruling in Barbara v. Trump, confers citizenship ​to those born in the United States who are “subject to the jurisdiction thereof.”

Following that decision, Trump signed a new order on Aug 6 that took particular aim at “birth tourism,” in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children ‌can ⁠obtain automatic citizenship.

Citizenship would also be denied to children if one of their parents works for foreign governments in the United States, engages in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an “alien enemy.”

After he signed that order, lawyers pursuing a class-action lawsuit on behalf of babies who would be deprived citizenship under Trump’s 2025 order asked Boardman to block enforcement of the Republican president’s newest order, and ensure their clients’ citizenship continued to be honoured.

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Joe Biden, agreed to do so, saying the latest order “is almost certainly unconstitutional as applied to the certified class for the simple reason that the Supreme Court in Barbara already decided that the children in the class are citizens at birth.”

“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” she wrote.

Her order bars agencies including the US Department of State, the US Department of Homeland Security, and the Social Security Administration from taking any action to interfere with, deny or fail to recognise citizenship of people covered by the class action.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The plaintiffs included the immigrant rights groups CASA and Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, which in 2025 convinced Boardman to become one of four lower-court judges to block Trump’s initial order prior to the Supreme Court ruling.

“Immigrant families should not have to come back to court to defend the rights of their US-born children and others whose citizenship is being questioned by a new executive order,” Conchita Cruz, co-executive director of the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, said in a statement.

Justice Department attorneys argued that an injunction was inappropriate in this case, as Trump’s order was more narrow than the sweeping one the plaintiffs first sued over.

They also called the lawsuit premature, saying federal agencies had yet to issue the necessary public guidance detailing how the president’s directive would be implemented, which they are expected to do by Sept 5.

Any legal challenge should wait until then, the administration argued.

But Boardman said an injunction was needed now, saying that while the Justice Department claimed the order would be applied only prospectively, by its plain terms it “applies to all children who meet its criteria, regardless of when they were born.”

“This Court must, once again, preliminarily enjoin enforcement of the President’s most recent attempt to strip the right to citizenship from them,” she wrote.

While Boardman blocked enforcement of Trump’s order, she said agencies could still issue guidance on how Trump’s order would be implemented.

Reuters reported on Sept 1 that the US State Department had drafted proposed guidance requiring parents applying for passports for their children to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status in order to implement that executive order. REUTERS

text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — An immigrant rights group sued the Trump administration Wednesday to block the U.S. Department of Homeland Security from using federal databases that it alleged are being used to target naturalized citizens who are eligible to vote.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court in Washington on behalf of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, alleges that DHS and the U.S. Justice Department are interfering with fair elections by using inaccurate federal databases in an attempt to buttress allegations of voter fraud.

The federal government is engaging in an “attack on the freedom to vote,” Angelica Salas, the coalition’s executive director, said at a downtown Los Angeles news conference. “This is voter intimidation.”

The lawsuit — filed on behalf of the coalition by the UCLA Voting Rights Project — becomes part of a swirl of legal moves that states, including California, have taken to fend off federal actions that threaten to create confusion during the midterms.

“It’s not an accident the federal government is trying to interfere with the right to vote. ... They believe they can intimidate naturalized U.S. citizens,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for California governor who is acting as a senior adviser to the voting project.

Part of a broader effort to search for noncitizens on voter rolls

The lawsuit alleges that the administration might be comparing voter rolls with undisclosed government databases. Those systems can include outdated information and be riddled with errors, it said, and could produce inaccurate results that disproportionately affect naturalized voters.

“Comparing government databases to try and arrive at a list of noncitizen registrants has been shown to result in erroneous data,” the lawsuit said. “Congress has never authorized such activities and in fact has ... prohibited invasion of voter privacy through government data matches in this way.”

The Trump administration has been targeting noncitizen voting to allege it could be a source of significant fraud during the midterm elections, even though actual voting by people who are not citizens is rare. He is pushing for the U.S. Postal Service to send mail ballots only to voters verified as U.S. citizens, and his Justice Department has sued to force the release of detailed voter data in 30 states and the District of Columbia, though it has not yet succeeded in those cases.

Asked to respond to the lawsuit, a DHS spokesperson said in an email: “The department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems. It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”

“DHS is laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens,” the statement added.

Judge had previously halted use of a federal citizenship database

In June, a federal judge ruled that a recently revamped version of a federal tool can no longer be used, which critics had referred to as an unlawful centralized federal database of voter information.

U.S. District Court Judge Sparkle L. Sooknanan sided with advocacy groups that argued the recent upgrades to the program, called Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, aggregated Americans’ sensitive personal data in a way that could result in voters being wrongly purged from voter rolls.

The lawsuit said it isn’t clear if the administration used that system to generate projections about noncitizens on voting rolls in the states or if other unknown datasets were involved.

By May, the Trump administration had run millions of voter registrations through government databases to determine their eligibility, a process that critics feared could purge valid voters from the rolls before the November elections. At least 67 million registrations, primarily from Republican-controlled states, have gone through a beefed-up verification program, or SAVE, at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, and tens of thousands of those have been flagged as potential noncitizens or people who have died.

State officials push back against DHS noncitizen claims

Specifically, the lawsuit by the immigrant rights group asks the court to stop the administration from pursuing a review of California’s voter list and to rescind the letter sent to the state requesting voter information. It also asks the court to declare the administration’s actions unconstitutional.

Trump’s Department of Homeland Security is claiming without providing evidence that 250,000 noncitizens might be on the rolls in just four states, including 190,832 in California.

California’s secretary of state, Democrat Shirley Weber, said in response, “I have serious doubts about the reliability of your data and accuracy of your claims, since my office has not shared our statewide voter registration list with DHS or any other federal agency or official.”

According to the lawsuit, federal officials have not disclosed evidence supporting those figures.

title: 'A perfect tool for abuse.' Why experts are concerned about ICE's $17 million electric shock ... - PBS
description:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents may soon be outfitted with electric shock gloves that can deliver painful jolts when they come in contact with a person's skin.
But the nearly $17 million contract for 6,000 pairs of gloves comes as ICE officers' use of force is facing increased scrutiny.
California's legislature swiftly passed a bill on Monday in reaction to the Trump administration's move, banning law enforcement officers from using electric shock gloves.
In February, a federal judge struck down a California law that would have banned ICE officers from wearing face masks.
Several Democratic senators have written DHS letters voicing their opposition to the electric shock gloves.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents may soon be outfitted with electric shock gloves that can deliver painful jolts when they come in contact with a person's skin. While ICE says the new gear will help agents deescalate situations with detainees or protesters without relying on "higher levels of force," Democrats in Congress and civil rights advocates are pushing back, in no small measure because of the agency's history of deadly clashes.

"ICE requires a low-impact tool for its officers and agents to utilize in cases where an individual is resisting arrest or otherwise represents a clear threat to officers and agents," the August contract justification said. "It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties."

White House border czar Tom Homan has argued the gloves could help avert deadly encounters.

"It's another device to help someone get compliant when they are not," Homan said in an Aug. 13 Fox News interview. "You can't just go from 0 to 100, right, and the first thing you go for is lethal force."

But the nearly $17 million contract for 6,000 pairs of gloves comes as ICE officers' use of force is facing increased scrutiny.

"It's a terrible idea for an agency with this level of violence, a record of dishonesty and its use of force records, and just a general lack of accountability structures to get this technology," said Katherine Hawkins, senior legal analyst at the Project on Government Oversight.

California's legislature swiftly passed a bill on Monday in reaction to the Trump administration's move, banning law enforcement officers from using electric shock gloves. Local police agencies have opposed the bill, saying the gloves are an important deescalation tool.

Whether California will successfully limit ICE agents from wearing the gloves is unclear. In February, a federal judge struck down a California law that would have banned ICE officers from wearing face masks.

Here's what to know about the gloves and the concerns surrounding them.

How do the gloves work?

The six-month, no-bid contract was awarded to Compliant Technologies LLC, a Kentucky-based company that makes products for law enforcement.

According to the company's website, the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, or G.L.O.V.E., includes a button officers press to activate. The electrical shock is emitted when the gloves come in contact with a person's bare skin.

The company has referred to the gloves, which cost $2,400 a pair, as a "pain compliance tool."

READ MORE: AP report: ICE plans to give its officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks

The product's user manual recommends not using it on elderly people, small children, pregnant women and "the severely handicapped." It also notes that the gloves may contribute to death or serious injury, and the electric shock can increase blood pressure, heart rate and adrenaline and can cause changes in heart rhythm.

The manual also says the gloves should not be deployed against verbal defiance or "belligerence" or as a form of punishment or torture.

Some local law enforcement agencies have already deployed the devices. In Dallas, KDFW reported that trained senior supervisors in Tarrant County Jail have been using the gloves for a year when inmates physically resist. Tarrant County Sheriff Bill Waybourn said the gloves have been "successfully" used a few times.

Compliant Technologies president Dan De La Cruz said in a podcast interview that his company's product is "so benign and humane that nobody gets hurt."

But the Associated Press reported that there is a pending lawsuit in Kentucky following the death of a 43-year-old man after being shocked 27 times with the gloves and another 13 times with a Taser at the Madison County Detention Center.

ICE hasn't detailed when or by whom the gloves will be used

The Department of Homeland Security hasn't published detailed plans about who at ICE will have access to the gloves, what training will be required to use them or what oversight measures will be implemented for their use. DHS did not respond to PBS News' request for comment.

Several Democratic senators have written DHS letters voicing their opposition to the electric shock gloves. The senators have requested ICE make public training requirements and "establish a robust system for documenting and reviewing every deployment and instance of use."

WATCH: ICE shootings spark outrage, protests across the country demanding accountability

Christopher Schneider, a sociology professor at Brandon University who studies policing, described the technology's rollout as "problematic."

He said ICE hasn't explained how its officers who are out in the field will know whether someone is pregnant or has a pacemaker and therefore should not have the gloves used on them. This could lead to "adverse consequences," he said.

WATCH: Minnesota leaders and protesters push for accountability after ICE shooting

Schneider also noted that it's unclear whether there are oversight mechanisms that will require officers to detail when and why they used the gloves. The gloves' user manual says they include a memory card that stores data when the gloves are activated.

"They are sort of a perfect tool for abuse," Schneider said, especially if they're used behind closed doors.

He said the gloves, which don't leave marks on people's skin, may make the "use of force more visually appealing," compared with other methods like a baton, Taser or gun.

Schneider said he believes the acquisition of the gloves is connected to ICE's move to equip its officers with body cameras in the next few months. The agency's policy says video will only be released when it's in the agency's best interest, according to the Associated Press.

READ MORE: ICE will only release body camera video when in agency's 'best interests,' policy says

During a demonstration of his company's shock gloves, De La Cruz said if a suspect is refusing to give law enforcement their hands to get handcuffed, agents are typically "forced to strike them, dig their knees into them, do multiple things. None of this looks good on camera."

He then uses the glove on a person's back.

"That was horrible, but you're not hurt," De La Cruz said. "And everything they saw on camera, I didn't strike you, I didn't do anything."

Civil rights advocates criticize ICE's lack of accountability

Experts in civil rights and government oversight who spoke with PBS News raised the lack of oversight and accountability as a central concern over ICE's eventual deployment of the electric shock gloves.

"We certainly don't have any assurance that if shock gloves are used on people and it results in severe injury, that ICE is actually gonna investigate that and tell the truth about it," said Naureen Shah, who leads immigration policy at the American Civil Liberties Union.

A boost in ICE hiring has also led to scaled-back training for new recruits, which further intensifies advocates' concerns over the new technology.

WATCH: Deadly shootings by ICE officers renew scrutiny of recruitment and training

Hawkins said the lack of accountability has "gotten particularly bad," under President Donald Trump's administration. Use of force increased "dramatically" in early 2025, according to a report by American Oversight, a government watchdog nonprofit.

While use of force by ICE can be subjected to a civil rights review and prosecution, Hawkins said, "it is very, very difficult to hold officers accountable at the best of times and even more so now."

PBS News multiplatform reporter Tim McPhillips contributed reporting for this story.

title: Two pastors detained, a student dead: Haitians in Ohio turn to faith amid fear of ICE
description:
Asked to speak, she took the microphone at Champion City Church.
After the arrests of two Haitian pastors, Adrien and Julio Dumano, local Haitian leaders put out a call for support.
More than 400 people responded — many of them faith leaders, some traveling from as far as Minnesota and Florida — to stand with Springfield.
Standing alongside the road, visiting faith leaders waved American flags and held signs that said, "Release Pastors Julio and Joubert" and "Jesus loves Haitians."
"We are not powerless," said Louis, one of the Haitian leaders who invited clergy to Springfield this weekend.
text:
Only days after two Haitian pastors were detained by federal immigration agents in Springfield, Ohio, the wife of one of the pastors, Denise Adrien Gedeon, arrived at a Friday (Aug. 28) evening vigil in support of Haitians in the embattled city.

Asked to speak, she took the microphone at Champion City Church. Her voice trembling, eyes closed and hand raised, she began to sing: "We give you all the glory. We worship you our Lord, you are worthy to be praised."

Then she spoke in Haitian Creole about her faith and God, with Viles Dorsainvil, a Haitian community leader and pastor, interpreting. "Despite everything, despite the difficult time, we believe in him, and we believe he will see us through," she said, adding she did not want money or food — just the return of her husband, Joubert Adrien, whom she met singing in a church choir in Haiti in 1999. He was detained Aug. 20.

Gedeon's plea was part of an especially turbulent week in Springfield, Ohio. After the arrests of two Haitian pastors, Adrien and Julio Dumano, local Haitian leaders put out a call for support. More than 400 people responded — many of them faith leaders, some traveling from as far as Minnesota and Florida — to stand with Springfield. Three days after Gedeon's plea, Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old Haitian college student, died in what his family is describing as a suicide.

Since the U.S. government removed temporary protected status for Haitians a few weeks ago, the Ohio city has been besieged by daily ICE raids, with over 30 Haitians detained by ICE, according to the Haitian Support Center, a nonprofit that assists Haitian nationals in Springfield. The organization estimates that ICE has outfitted more than 100 people with ankle monitors to track their whereabouts.

With about 10,000 Haitians living in the city of 58,000, many have been hiding out in their homes, fearing detainment. A small contingent of local Haitian community leaders, several pastors themselves, braved Friday's vigil. Many Haitian churches sat empty Sunday morning.

During the weekend, hundreds of volunteers — Baptists, Unitarian Universalists, Mennonites, Quakers and others — packed food boxes for Haitians in hiding, held phone drives asking elected officials to release the pastors and stood outside Haitian churches on Sunday morning to advocate for Haitians' right to worship without fear.

That fear has been fueled by the flurry of rapid ICE raids happening throughout the city. Around 9 a.m. on Aug. 20, Gedeon said that she and her husband, Adrien, were riding in a car with Adrien's cousin and his wife. They had just pulled out of a gas station when a car sped in front of them and slammed on the brakes. Four other cars surrounded their vehicle.

"At that time, I kept saying, ‘Please God, let us go, free us, please God, let us go,'" Gedeon recalled, speaking through an interpreter. Several masked officers she identified as ICE agents approached the vehicle and asked to see IDs and work permits, she said. The officers handcuffed the two men. Gedeon, who cried out to her husband before he was taken away, said she hasn't seen him since.

A father of two living in the U.S. for five years, Adrien is the Haitian ministry pastor at High Street Church, a Nazarene congregation in Springfield. Local advocates say he has no criminal history and no final order of removal. The couple had temporary protected status and have pending asylum cases, according to Gedeon.

Speaking to RNS on the back steps of High Street Church, head Pastor Marty Dennis explained that Adrien was part of a group of Haitians who visited his church four years ago seeking a place to worship in Haitian Creole. What began as 15 Haitians worshipping in a living room grew to over 100 people meeting in the church gymnasium, while Dennis' congregation held worship in their sanctuary.

Now the gym is empty. The Haitian congregants are worshipping remotely while Adrien is held in Butler County Jail, about an hour from Springfield. Even in prison, Dennis and Gedeon said, Adrien is ministering to those around him. "He loves God more than life itself," said Dennis. "I couldn't imagine doing life without him."

Gedeon, with the loss of her work permit, now stays at home, caring for their two kids, ages 7 and 14, alone. Last week, their youngest celebrated her seventh birthday without her father. But she said she leans on her faith in God, saying, "Maybe this happened for good reason, and the good reason was for him to go in that detention center, preach to people, be close to people, and give them hope."

Michaelle Louis, a Haitian community organizer with Undivided — one of the several faith groups behind the week's gathering of faith leaders — said ICE is deliberately detaining men — "the head of the family." The idea is, she said, "if they deport the husband, the rest of the family is going to follow."

Carl Ruby, pastor of Central Christian Church and founder of G92, a nonprofit organization that advocates for immigrants, said he learned in meetings with regional and national ICE leaders that their aim is to make living in the U.S. unbearable for Haitians.

"I was surprised how candid they were," said Ruby. "They said … ‘We're going to make life as miserable as possible.'"

Though Springfield doesn't have the largest Haitian population in the U.S., pro-immigrant organizers say their city has been a political target since then-candidate Donald Trump and his running mate, J.D. Vance, spread falsehoods about the city's Haitians eating pets in the run-up to the 2024 presidential election. Nearly two years later, Haitians in Springfield said the ankle monitors, which many compared to slave shackles, are part of a Springfield-specific ICE experiment.

On Monday, 20-year-old Pierre Damas Bel, a pre-med student and soccer player at Wright State University, was fatally struck by a tractor-trailer. Bel's family is describing his death as a suicide. Ohio State Highway Patrol called it "an open investigation."

In a statement written by Bel's father after his son's death, he said his son had taken two trips to Cincinnati to plead with officers to remove his ankle monitor, which was visible when he played soccer. "After my son was outfitted with this ankle monitor, he felt like he was treated like an animal," he wrote. The statement says Bel's classmates bullied him because of the monitor.

A spokesperson for Wright State University said the university was "heartbroken" about the death of Bel. The university has "no confirmed information regarding complaints or investigations into bullying related to the student," the spokesperson said in a statement, adding that "we remain dedicated to providing a campus community where every student feels safe, supported, included and welcomed."

Ruby, who was with Bel's parents Monday night, said he has seen "the extremes" in recent weeks.

"I believe in a good God who will eventually make all things right, who will punish evil and restore justice, but living in the here and now is really hard," he said. One day he gathered with hundreds to protest ICE's immigration policy. The next day, he said, he listened to "the sobs and screams" of Bel's parents.

"We need a revival of the spirit of the prophets where people of faith demand justice in their government and in their churches," he said.

On Sunday morning, dozens of clergy stood outside First Haitian Evangelical Church of Springfield, one of the city's largest Haitian congregations and home to Pastor Julio Dumano, an assistant pastor at the church who was detained on Aug. 25. The whereabouts of Dumano, who was described by fellow clergy as a "godly man," are currently unknown.

Standing alongside the road, visiting faith leaders waved American flags and held signs that said, "Release Pastors Julio and Joubert" and "Jesus loves Haitians."

Inside, nearly 40 volunteers and faith leaders sat in chairs alongside Haitian congregants, singing "How Great Thou Art" in Haitian Creole and in English. Though the once-packed church had only a few-dozen Haitian members that Sunday, their enthusiasm wasn't diminished. The congregants, wearing suits, dresses and heels in bright colors, danced in worship and welcomed their visitors with enthusiasm.

"Thank you so much for coming," Pastor Reginald Silencieux said warmly from the podium. "When I see your presence, it's very encouraging. When Haitian people see you, they can see Jesus is alive. Amen?"

Hours later, over 400 people made their way to City Hall, where they shared an outdoor potluck, sang "We Shall Overcome" and heard remarks from local leaders. Speakers made three demands of ICE, the Department of Homeland Security and elected officials: release the pastors, stop outfitting Haitians with ankle monitors and stop "treating them inhumanely because of their nationality and the color of their skin."

"We're making these demands in the name of Christ," Ruby said at the rally.

At the conclusion of Sunday's event, Haitian pastor Bernadette Dor-Dominique invited attendees to march seven times around City Hall. She explained that the "Jericho march" was a reference to the biblical book of Joshua, which says God tore down the walls of Jericho after the Israelites marched around the city for seven days.

"It is a symbolic act of faith, unity, perseverance and trust in God when the situation appears impossible," said Dor-Dominique. "We are walking against fear and division, standing together as one community."

Since Springfield's Haitian population became national news during the 2024 campaign, the city has endured bomb threats, neo-Nazi rallies and now an ICE surge. But pro-immigrant advocates, like Louis, say the city's story remains one of resilience and faith.

"We are not powerless," said Louis, one of the Haitian leaders who invited clergy to Springfield this weekend.

Ruby, for his part, said he was "encouraged" by the number of volunteers who showed up Sunday, but "until the entire church practices a faith that looks like Jesus, we have a lot of work to do."

text:
LITTLE ROCK, Ark. — Mitchell Best, 43, was sentenced to 60 years in federal prison for producing child sexual abuse material depicting a child under the age of five. Best was indicted July 2, 2024, on five counts of production of child sexual abuse material, one count of distribution of child sexual abuse material and one count of possession of child sexual abuse material. He pleaded guilty Feb. 18, 2026, to two production counts and was sentenced to two consecutive 30-year federal prison terms. ICE’s Homeland Security Investigations conducted the probe.

Best was also sentenced in December 2024 to 30 years in state prison for rape. The judge in the case ordered 10 years of Best’s federal sentence to run concurrently with his state sentence; Best then will serve his remaining 50 years.

“Our investigation and the sentence for these heinous crimes reaffirms HSI’s commitment to identifying and bringing those who exploit our most vulnerable to justice,” said acting HSI New Orleans Special Agent in Charge Matt Wright. “This outcome was only possible through the seamless collaboration between our special agents, the Arkansas State Police and the Cabot Police Department. We will continue to leverage every resource at our disposal to investigate these crimes and work alongside our partners to protect children from such predators."

On April 2, 2024, HSI and officers from the Cabot Police Department executed a search warrant at Best’s home. Agents found multiple files of child sexual abuse material, including images and videos that depicted Best sexually assaulting a young child, during a forensic examination of his phone.

The investigation was conducted by HSI with assistance from the Arkansas State Police and the Cabot Police Department. This case was prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Arkansas Kristin Bryant.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse.

title: Judge 'hesitant' on where to draw the line in lawsuit over immigration enforcement tactics
description:

Ellis said she thought at the time it was well within her role as a judge.
But Ellis said she’s “a little hesitant to wade into” drawing the line between law enforcement and coercion.
The suit seeks a judicial order limiting these and other practices, including conducting immigration enforcement operations from “sensitive” areas such as schools, courthouses and hospitals, and limiting the use of “biometric” scanning of fingerprints and other personal information.

text:
With the anniversary of Operation Midway Blitz less than a week away, the militarized tactics of immigration agents that roiled Chicago last fall were once again front and center in federal court on Wednesday as a judge weighs the merits of a lawsuit alleging the Trump administration’s policies are unconstitutional.

But U.S. District Judge Sara Ellis, who last November issued a landmark preliminary injunction limiting the use of force by immigration agents, seemed more skeptical this time around about her ability to police the Justice Department’s enforcement of immigration laws, particularly in light of an appellate court ruling that she’d overstepped her authority.

“Clearly under the separation of powers, I cannot manage the Executive Branch,” Ellis told the parties during the nearly four hours of arguments. “I think I’d said that before, but I’ve been told it again.”

Ellis harked back to her dramatic decision in a lawsuit brought by the Chicago Headline Club to force then-Border Patrol Cmdr. Greg Bovino, who headed the Midway Blitz operation, to come to court and explain why her orders limiting tear gas and other uses of force on protesters were obviously not being followed.

Ellis said she thought at the time it was well within her role as a judge. But the 7th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals later overruled her, calling it a “constitutionally suspect” violation of the separation of powers.

“I certainly thought that having Mr. Bovino come into court and…demonstrate ‘this is how I complied with this order’ was a way of enforcing an order that I had the right to make,” Ellis said. “There was difference of opinion on whether that violated the separation of powers, and I think that is illustrative of how tricky that can be.”

The plaintiffs have alleged the Justice Department’s tactics were part of a campaign to coerce Illinois and Chicago to abandon sanctuary policies protecting immigrants, in violation of the Tenth Amendment.

But Ellis said she’s “a little hesitant to wade into” drawing the line between law enforcement and coercion. “At what point do I step out of my lane?” she said.

The judge’s comments came as she weighs the government’s motion to dismiss a lawsuit filed jointly by the Illinois Attorney General’s Office and city of Chicago in January alleging a broad swath of illegal actions during the Trump administration’s controversial deportation campaign.

The 103-page lawsuit — which was filed after the Chicago Headline Club case was dismissed — alleged immigration agents acted more like an occupying military force than law enforcement during Midway Blitz, terrorizing neighborhoods with “roving patrols,” illegally switching out license plates, randomly stopping people to question them about their citizenship, and making warrantless arrests.

The suit seeks a judicial order limiting these and other practices, including conducting immigration enforcement operations from “sensitive” areas such as schools, courthouses and hospitals, and limiting the use of “biometric” scanning of fingerprints and other personal information.

Justice Department lawyers argue that the plaintiffs lack standing on almost every count, pointing out Operation Midway Blitz was long over by the time the lawsuit was filed and there was no plausible or imminent threat of harm to citizens.

The government’s motion to dismiss also argued that there had been no showing that any “core” activities of the state or city were disrupted due to the immigration enforcement tactics — another way in which the plaintiffs have alleged ongoing harm.

At the outset of Wednesday’s hearing, Ellis questioned attorney Paul Berks, who represents Attorney General Kwame Raoul’s office, the potential harm to Illinois citizens going forward, since the surge of agents ended months ago and it would be mere speculation to say it’s going to return.

“If we’re looking at sort of past is prologue, it seems as though this surge and enforcement happens in one area, and then moves on to another and another and another, without necessarily returning,” Ellis said, noting that after leaving Chicago, agents landed in North Carolina and Minnesota. “So this is where I’m struggling on standing. I can’t really look backwards, necessarily. I have to have some evidence that there is going to be imminent harm in the future.”

Berks said that enhanced immigration enforcement continues in and around Chicago to this day, including increased arrests at courthouses and other co-called “sensitive locations.”

He also cited the administration’s own statements that they were not done with Chicago. Among them: a call by Trump himself on Truth Social for immigration officials “to do all in their power” to effect “the single largest Mass Deportation Program in History” in Democratic power centers like Chicago.

“The motivation is there,” Berks said. “The policies are still in place. The threats have been made…The fact that they haven’t returned to Chicago yet is not evidence that they’re not going to return to Chicago.”

Ellis said she’d rule on the motion to dismiss at the next hearing Nov. 17.

The lawsuit is one of several that are still pending at the Dirksen U.S. Courthouse nearly a year after Operation Midway Blitz began in earnest on Sept. 8, 2025, a roughly two-month surge that led to nearly daily clashes in the streets between protesters and heavily armed agents, who often used tear gas, pepper spray balls, and rubber bullets on crowds.

In October, Ellis held a marathon hearing in the case brought by the Chicago Headline Club before issuing a landmark preliminary injunction limiting such practices. She found in her scathing opinion that not only had agents used inappropriate force, but that immigration leaders, including Bovino, had lied about it under oath.

But Ellis’ injunction was later stayed by the 7th Circuit, and the plaintiffs moved to dismiss the suit without prejudice as a tactical maneuver, which the judge granted.

In March, a 7th Circuit panel voted 2-1 to order what’s known as “vacatur,” which essentially treated Ellis’ preliminary injunction ruling as though it never existed. In the 15-page majority opinion, the judges wrote that Ellis, “working on a highly compressed timeline … granted an overbroad, constitutionally suspect injunction.”

The majority was particularly critical of Ellis for dismissing the lawsuit “without prejudice” even though the parties didn’t ask for it, leaving the door open for plaintiffs to refile the case at some point down the road.

By then, Ellis had already granted a request from lawyers for Illinois and Chicago to preside over their suit — over the strenuous objection of the Justice Department.

Ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, the plaintiffs filed a motion for new discovery into ongoing immigration enforcement efforts in the Chicago area, including information from the past three months about deployment of tear gas, enforcement actions at courthouses and other sensitive locations, warrantless arrests, and “misuse of license plates,” court records show.

text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio —

A Wright State University student's death by suicide is a mournful reality for the university and for Springfield's Haitian community.

Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old first-year student at Wright State, died on Monday. His family said he was overwhelmed by bullying and shame after immigration agents placed an ankle monitor on him in July.

Bel, an honor roll athlete, had been recruited to play soccer at Wittenberg University but lost his roster spot after receiving the monitor.

"He felt so humiliated," said Viles Dorsainvil, executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield. "The monitor had just stopped everything."

Despite the setback, Bel enrolled at Wright State to continue his education and pursue his dream of becoming a doctor.

Wright State University President Sue Edwards expressed sorrow over Bel's death, saying, "We are heartbroken by this devastating loss. Pierre was an active honors student who was passionate about soccer and was already actively engaged in his classes and the campus community. The University mourns the death of Pierre and extends our deepest condolences to his family, friends and loved ones during this unimaginably difficult time."

Even before Bel's death, frustration over the use of ankle monitors had been growing in Springfield's Haitian community, where many have lost their temporary protected status and live in fear of ICE agents. On Friday, faith leaders and Springfield NAACP President Denise Williams rallied for change.

"Unshackle Springfield. Unshackle Springfield," Williams said.

Bel's father said his son died after throwing himself in front of a semi-truck on Interstate 70, overwhelmed by taunts from classmates about the ankle monitor.

"It was devastating news for us," Dorsainvil said.

Dorsainvil hopes Bel's death will lead to policy changes in Washington. "I am calling upon the administration all the time, upon the policymakers to review the policies, because behind them are real human lives. If they can do that, I think that it would be good for the country," he said.

Professors and students at Wright State and residents in Springfield are now navigating the grieving process. Wright State has made counseling available for students, while the Haitian Support Network is planning a memorial for Bel next week.

The investigation into Bel's death remains open. Meanwhile, Dorsainvil is working with a local mental health expert to organize group sessions for young Haitians affected by the tragedy.

text:
The Justice Department sanctioned a powerful new legal tool the Trump administration can use to compel states to assist with the White House’s crackdown on immigration.

The Tuesday opinion by the Office of Legal Counsel sets a framework for the federal government to revoke future welfare grants from states that refuse to report immigrants that did not enter the nation lawfully — another example of the administration threatening to revoke federal funding to force states to provide more data and information about the immigrants who live there.

Funding for federal social services, like Social Security and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, have largely been dispensed at the discretion of the states since Congress overhauled the national welfare system in 1996. That revamp narrowed certain state reporting requirements in an effort to prevent noncitizens from taking welfare benefits. Previous administrations have agreed that the reporting burden falls only on the specific state agencies that dispense those funds.

The Office of Legal Counsel, which provides legal guidance to the executive branch, reversed that precedent this week.

Trending

Dusting off the decades-old, Clinton-era welfare law, Deputy Assistant Attorney General Joshua Craddock concluded in his 19-page opinion that the previous reporting requirements were too “narrow.”

Specifically, Craddock asserts that all agencies in a state that receives welfare grants — which includes every state in the union, as well as the District of Columbia and U.S. territories — must now report immigrants they believe illegally came to the country.

The office’s announcement relies on a revamped interpretation of the word “state” under the 1996 law, retooling it to encompass “all component agencies,” not just the specific agency administering federal benefits.

“The mandatory reporting obligations … thus apply to all agencies within a state that participates in the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and Supplemental Security Income programs subject to those requirements,” Craddock wrote.

The DOJ said states not currently compliant with the reporting requirements will not lose federal funding that has already been allocated, but future dollars would be jeopardized should state agencies refuse to report undocumented immigrants.

“States remain free to reevaluate their participation in TANF or SSI going forward in view of today’s opinion,” Craddock wrote.

Trump has frequently attempted to withhold federal dollars as a way to ensure so-called sanctuary states and jurisdictions comply with his mass-deportation agenda, but federal judges have consistently ruled against him. More than a dozen states and D.C. have enacted policies aimed at restricting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. It is unclear how the new federal precedent will clash with those state-level mandates, though some may choose to sue the administration over its new directive.

text:
LOS ANGELES — The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration on Wednesday, alleging the federal government is illegally targeting non-U.S. born citizens to prevent them from exercising their legal right to vote.

Filed against the Department of Homeland Security, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Attorney General Todd Blanche, the suit contends they are interfering with the right of individual states to conduct free and fair elections.

“Naturalized citizens are Americans,” CHIRLA executive director Angelica Salas said at a news conference announcing the lawsuit in downtown Los Angeles on Wednesday. “They took the oath. They earned their citizenship, and they have the same rights as every other American citizen.”

CHIRLA director of organizing and naturalized U.S. citizen, Pedro Trujillo, is also a plaintiff in the lawsuit “because I do not want this federal administration to get away with their attempts at voter intimidation or even worse: creating second-class citizenship where naturalized citizens are not given the rights they have earned,” he said.

Trujillo was brought to the United States by his parents when he was six years old, attended public school, graduated from a state university and applied for, and became, a U.S. citizen after 20 years of being undocumented, he said.

The lawsuit is one of several that has been filed against the Trump administration after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in March “Ensuring Citizenship and Integrity in Federal Elections,” which directed the Department of Homeland Security, in partnership with the Social Security Administration, to develop an approved list of absentee voters.

After California and several other states refused to hand over their voter rolls, the Department of Justice sent letters to state election officials in July saying they would be criminally prosecuted if they knowingly retained noncitizens on their rolls, while the Department of Homeland Security said it would withhold Federal Emergency Management Agency funds from states that hadn’t used a DHS system to verify the citizenship of individuals on their voter rolls.

Filed Wednesday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, the CHIRLA complaint centers on a letter the Trump administration sent to California officials alleging that more than 190,000 non-citizens are registered to vote in the state.

“Methodology for arriving at this figure has never been provided, and it is almost certainly widely incorrect,” the complaint says.

UCLA Voting Rights Projects Senior Data Scientist Michael Rios said at Wednesday’s news conference that efforts to compare databases, such as the federal government is seeking to do with state voter files, are problematic.

“Names can be misspelled, they can be shortened, they change after marriage, they can be entered differently between databases… There could be issues of capitalization, punctuation and spacing,” Rios said.

“Unless databases have a unique identifier to merge them by, a similar name, birthdate, or address cannot establish that two records represent the same person,” he added. “That’s why you have to extremely careful in methodologies and validation efforts before drawing conclusions.”

The CHIRLA lawsuit is asking the court to declare the Trump administration’s voter list matching unconstitutional and unlawful and to stop the practice.

“DHS is laser focused on prosecuting and removing aliens who vote and preventing the dilution of the votes of U.S. citizens,” a DHS spokesperson told Spectrum News.

“We have repeatedly demonstrated that illegal aliens can and do vote in our elections,” the spokesperson added. “Under President Trump, Homeland Security Investigations is committed to restoring integrity to our election systems and ensuring that American citizens, and only American citizens, are electing American leaders.”

Noncitizen voting in any state is “extremely small,” according to the Center for Election Innovation & Research, which found that “claims about possible noncitizen registrations and voting allege vanishingly small numbers. Even the largest claims (which are the most likely to be severe overestimates) never allege numbers that are more than roughly one-tenth of one percent of the number of active registered voters in the state.”

Saudi Arabia is in a volatile region that has seen the collapse of many dictatorships that were thought to be stable.
Now, the Trump Administration is green-lighting an uncontrolled nuclear program for Saudi Arabia.
It was the policy of the first Trump Administration that a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia needed to include the Gold Standard and Additional Protocol provisions.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio recognized the need for these safeguards years ago when he joined me in introducing the Saudi Nuclear Nonproliferation Act in 2016, and I applaud Senator Kennedy (R-LA) for registering his opposition to this no-safeguards Saudi nuclear deal last month.
text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman Brad Sherman (CA-32), senior member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, issued the following statement after reviewing the proposed U.S.-Saudi Arabia Section 123 Agreement for peaceful nuclear cooperation submitted to Congress by the Trump Administration:

“I have read the proposed 123 Agreement that the Trump Administration has sent to Congress, both the unclassified and classified portions. The classified portion of the Agreement includes a blank page labeled “to be filled in later.” Clearly the Trump Administration has not submitted the Agreement for review as required by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, which requires that Congress see the whole agreement.

I am profoundly disturbed by the path this agreement creates for a nuclear-armed Saudi Arabia.

This deal claims to facilitate peaceful nuclear technology for Saudi Arabia but intentionally excludes the very safeguards that determine whether or not a country with nuclear technology can use it to build nuclear weapons: the Gold Standard and Additional Protocol. Not only that, but this agreement explicitly allows uranium enrichment on Saudi soil under certain conditions. And only President Trump, not the Congress, will determine if those vague conditions have been met.

Crown Prince Mohammad Bin Salman has been clear about his intentions to pursue a nuclear weapon, and Saudi Arabia has already shown a willingness to advance down that path covertly by standing up an undeclared, Chinese-backed yellowcake-extraction facility just a few years ago.

Saudi Arabia is in a volatile region that has seen the collapse of many dictatorships that were thought to be stable. It was the United States that provided preliminary nuclear technology to Iran through the Atoms for Peace program when it was ruled by a friendly, pro-Western monarch – and all of the technology in the hands of the Shah in 1978 fell into the hands of the Ayatollah in 1979.

Today, we are fighting a war designed to prevent Iran from having an uncontrolled nuclear program. Now, the Trump Administration is green-lighting an uncontrolled nuclear program for Saudi Arabia. While the current Saudi government is far less problematic than the one in Tehran, no one knows who will be in power in Riyadh ten years from now. This region has seen the collapse of many dictatorships that were thought to be stable, and this deal gambles the nuclear security of the United States and the world on the very weak assumption that pro-Western leaders will continue to head Saudi Arabia in the decades to come.

A Saudi nuclear bomb would shred the nonproliferation regime of the last half century. Once Saudi Arabia has an uncontrolled nuclear program with America’s blessing, Egypt, Turkey, and perhaps South Korea and Brazil will not be far behind.

This should not be a Democratic or Republican issue – this is about American national security, and the United States’ longstanding bipartisan commitments to non-proliferation. It was the policy of the first Trump Administration that a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia needed to include the Gold Standard and Additional Protocol provisions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio recognized the need for these safeguards years ago when he joined me in introducing the Saudi Nuclear Nonproliferation Act in 2016, and I applaud Senator Kennedy (R-LA) for registering his opposition to this no-safeguards Saudi nuclear deal last month. Members of Congress – Republican and Democrat alike – must reject this deal with a Joint Resolution of Disapproval until the necessary safeguards are included.”
