text:
Article Insights

Recent legislative, regulatory, and litigation developments have affected Temporary Protected Status (TPS)-related employment authorization, with implications for ongoing work authorization.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed into law July 4, 2025, includes a provision limiting TPS-based employment authorization documents (EADs) to a maximum validity period of one year, or the duration of an individual’s TPS status, whichever is shorter. The OBBBA also directly curtails the previously available 540-day automatic extensions that many TPS holders relied upon. An interim final rule from the Department of Homeland Security issued Oct. 30, 2025, eliminated the regulatory basis for those 540-day automatic extensions going forward.

The Deadline for TPS EAD Extensions

For TPS beneficiaries who filed EAD renewal applications before July 22, 2025, and whose applications remained pending, automatic work authorization extensions expired on July 22, 2026, regardless of any later expiration date reflected on a Form I-797C receipt notice. This affected TPS holders from El Salvador, Sudan, Ukraine, and other designated countries that had been counting on extension end dates as late as October 2026.

The Court’s Decision Upholding the 1-Year EAD Cap

Litigation over these policies has produced mixed results. On July 21, 2026, a federal court in Massachusetts temporarily stayed certain United States Citizenship and Immigration Services policies, briefly preserving prior extension expiration dates. However, on Aug. 5, 2026, that same court largely sided with the government, upholding the one-year cap policy and rejecting arguments that it was procedurally flawed or impermissibly retroactive. The court confirmed that TPS beneficiaries from El Salvador, Sudan, and Ukraine are subject to the July 22, 2026, expiration of their 540-day extensions.

The court did grant limited relief on an unrelated policy involving consequences for asylum applicants who failed to pay the annual asylum fee, staying that provision pending further proceedings.

Employer Considerations: I-9 Reverification and E-Verify Compliance

Employers with TPS workers on their payroll may wish to take the following steps:

Audit I-9 records to identify EADs tied to TPS categories A12 or C19.

Verify whether those EADs were subject to a 540-day automatic extension that has now been cut short.

Complete I-9 reverification for any affected employees.

Monitor E-Verify for status updates reflecting the revised expiration dates.

A Note on Ongoing TPS Litigation for Other Designated Countries

Work authorization for TPS beneficiaries from certain other countries, including Burma (Myanmar), Ethiopia, Haiti, Somalia, South Sudan, Syria, and Yemen, may still be protected by separate court orders and pending litigation.

The content of this article is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter. Specialist advice should be sought about your specific circumstances.

text:
A 17-year-old Gainesville High School student-athlete, Sebastian Jimenez, was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Jimenez and his family were taken from their apartment on August 22, according to his football coach.

Jimenez and his mother are being held at a facility in Texas pending a bond hearing.

The community, including his football team and coach, has rallied to show support and seek legal help.

A Gainesville High School student-athlete has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to Gainesville High football coach Ashour Peera and athletic director Phillip Knight.

Sebastian Jimenez, a 17-year-old senior, was detained by ICE agents Aug. 22, along with his mother, stepfather and 28-year-old sister from their Gainesville apartment, according to Peera.

The Sun searched ICE’s “Online Detainee Locator System” for Jimenez but found no records. The website states that individuals under 18 cannot be searched in the database.

His mother – Anmary Mayela-Peroza – also did not appear in the website’s records. A call on Monday, Aug. 31, to the Miramar Sub Office, which handles ICE detentions in Florida, has not yet been returned.

Who is Sebastian Jimenez?

Jimenez plays football, soccer and baseball at Gainesville High. He was the kicker and punter for the Hurricanes in their season-opening game vs. Belleview on Aug. 21.

Peera is in his first season as GHS coach, but his son, Tyler, knew Jimenez, and Peera said Jimenez had been to his house before.

“He was the only player I knew at GHS when I arrived,” Peera said Aug. 28.

Since Jimenez’s detainment, GHS students are showing their support. Ahead of the Hurricanes’ Aug. 28 rivalry game against Buchholz at Citizens Field, the football team ran through a banner that had words of support for Jimenez.

The student section at the game also held a Venezuelan flag with Jimenez’s No. 17 jersey number on it. Peera said he considered wearing a shirt with Jimenez’s face on it during the contest.

Postgame, Peera spoke little of the game itself. Instead, he called attention to Jimenez.

“It’s not about football right now for us. It’s about getting him back safely and us doing him proud and giving the effort that he would want us to have,” Peera said.

How were Sebastian Jimenez and his family detained by ICE

A friend didn’t hear from Jimenez and his family on Aug. 22, the day after the opening football game, and that friend then emailed Peera.

On Aug. 23, Peera went to the family’s apartment and, as he arrived, Jimenez called him. Since then, Peera and Jimenez have spoken seven times on the phone, thanks to commissary funds Peera has provided.

Peera said the four family members were taken to an ICE detention facility in Jacksonville. Then, Jimenez and his mother were sent to the South Texas Family Residential Center in Dilley, Texas.

The current location of his sister and stepfather is unknown.

According to Peera, Jimenez, his mother and sister are Venezuelan. His stepfather is Brazilian.

The coach said the family moved to the U.S. when Jimenez was 7 years old. This came after his mother and sister had been kidnapped in Venezuela. The U.S. government began to allow asylum for Venezuelan citizens in 1998 when Hugo Chavez was elected, and Jimenez’s family had applied for it when their visa expired.

What’s next for Sebastian Jimenez and his family?

Jimenez and his mother are scheduled to have a hearing Sept. 8 at the Texas facility to determine their future, which could include a release on bond and a return to Gainesville.

Peera said that Jimenez sounded strong on the phone, but he could still sense fear in his voice.

Peera has reached out to several attorneys for help and to U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s office. Peera coached Rubio’s son – Anthony – at the University of Florida from 2023-25.

“We don’t understand why this would happen to a kid that’s been here over a decade, that’s such a good member of his community, plays three sports, is a member of clubs, and a great friend and teammate, why he would be taken from his home,” Peera said. “We’d really like to see if there is anyone who can help us in this situation to provide guidance, tell us how to approach it and figure out what options do we have?”

Trump’s ‘Blitz’ on Chicago targeting the ‘worst of the worst’ detained only 5 murderers in 68 days

Reporting by Lauren FitzPatrick and Alden Loury

text:
At least six people in California have died in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody during President Donald Trump’s second term — the highest number of deaths under a presidential administration in nearly two decades.

The data, sourced from government records and compiled by an immigration data analysis firm called Relevant Research, found that 56 people had died in ICE custody since the start of the current administration. That is roughly one person every 11 days.

In California, all six of the deaths occurred at hospitals and shortly after people had been at federal detention centers. Four of the deaths were of people held at the Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County. Two other people died after detainment at the Imperial Regional Detention Facility near the U.S. and Mexico border.

“Being in ICE custody is much broader than whether or not someone’s actually just physically inside of an immigrant detention facility,” said Austin Kocher, president of Relevant Research, at a Monday afternoon virtual news conference about the data.

Families of the deceased in five of the cases have alleged the facility or ICE failed to provide adequate medical care, according to media reports and an investigation by the California Department of Justice published in May.

The state DOJ investigation found that detention conditions had largely worsened as the federal administration’s mass deportation campaign led to “overcrowding and strained resources.” Dozens of news outlets have reported similar worsening conditions at detention facilities across the country.

“In a way, the complications of detention centers are bleeding out, to use unfortunately a very graphic and accurate metaphor, into all of these other medical facilities,” Kocher said.

Kocher, who is also a research fellow at American University’s Center for Latin American and Latino Studies, launched the “Detention Mortality Dashboard” earlier this month. The dashboard, using ICE records, shows that 289 people have died in ICE custody since October 2003. The data does not include deaths of people who were released from custody and later died from complications.

California accounts for 40 of the total deaths, which is second most in the nation after Texas. The two states are among the highest in total number of ICE detainees. In 2006, six people in California died in ICE custody — the most in any reported year for the state.

“This is not a problem that started with the Trump administration,” Kocher said.

As of this year, California has about 9,200 beds across eight U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities. All are operated by private companies and located in the southern half of the state.

Kocher said the data does not seek to answer why someone died in custody, noting that ICE announcements for deaths may be incomplete, inaccurate or framed to criminalize the person. He is also unable to evaluate the medical claims.

Following a death of a person in custody, ICE must issue an initial news release announcing the death. The agency then must publicize a more detailed report within 90 days. These reports have become shorter, less detailed and more dehumanizing under Trump’s second term, Kocher said.

“We’re not necessarily going to repeat those kinds of claims or repeat that kind of language, especially because we can’t verify it,” Kocher said.

The six people that died under Trump’s second term are Jose Guadalupe Ramos-Solano, Alberto Gutierrez-Reyes, Luis Yanez Cruz, Gabriel Garcia Aviles, Huabing Xie and Ismael Ayala-Uribe. All except Xie, of China, and Yanez Cruz, of Honduras, originated from Mexico.

This week, the California Legislature has advanced several detention-related bills to Gov. Gavin Newsom’s desk. Among the legislation are efforts to impose a 25% tax on the gross income of for-profit corporations that operate immigration detention facilities, prohibit the use of state-owned property for immigration enforcement and deny businesses involved with detention facilities from receiving state grants or loans.

Newsom has until Sept. 30 to sign or veto the bills.

text:
(Texas Tribune) — The third eyewitness to the fatal shooting of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston by an immigration officer last month has been released from federal detention.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials released Victor Salgado Araujo, who is Lorenzo’s brother, from custody Sunday morning, after his attorney filed several legal petitions including a federal suit claiming he is wrongfully being detained. The government also indicated it would likely approve his application for a temporary legal status since he is a witness to a potential crime.

He had been held in the Montgomery ICE Processing Center, which is north of Houston, since the July 7 shooting.

That morning, Victor Salgado Araujo sat in the front seat of his brother’s van as they picked up two fellow workers for a construction job, when ICE officers started following them in unmarked vehicles.

ICE initially said Lorenzo Salgado Araujo rammed their vehicles as he tried to flee and an officer shot him in self-defense. But Victor Salgado Araujo and the two other passengers disputed that account.

Victor Salgado Araujo’s release comes just days after Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare publicly said he plans to bring the case to a grand jury in the “next few weeks,” partly to force the release of more evidence. And because there is no body camera or dash camera footage of the shooting, his testimony as one of just three eyewitnesses is even more crucial to the understanding of what happened.

The other two eyewitnesses, Daniel Tirado Pantoja and Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, have already been released from ICE custody.

“Victor’s release is an important moment, but it is not the end of this fight,” his attorney, Ruby Powers, said in a statement. “The pursuit of truth, accountability, and justice for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo continues, and we remain steadfast in protecting Victor’s immigration rights and standing alongside him and his family.”

Ronaldo Salgado, Lorenzo’s son, similarly called his uncle’s release “a key step” in getting justice for his father.

“His first meal was chilaquiles from his favorite restaurant, just as his usual Sunday routine called for,” he added in a Facebook post. “He is now with family, finally able to process the tragic loss he witnessed and the nearly two months spent in detention.

text:
A small but committed group of protesters opposed to the Trump administration have become a familiar site on Saturdays at the intersection of East Putnam Ave and Indian Field Rd in Cos Cob.

While Indivisible Greenwich’s No Kings rallies have drawn over 1,000 people to the Havemeyer lawn, with officials including Governor Lamont and Attorney General Tong speaking, the grassroots demonstrators in Cos Cob stand out for their persistence.

For more than a year, and in all types of weather, the small group has appeared with handmade signs at the highly visible intersection for an hour every Saturday.

They count their support in honks.

Dan Edelstein from Old Greenwich said no permit was required for the weekly protests. Greenwich Police had stopped by to say the only rules were not to go in the street, not to impede traffic, and to always cross with the light.

“Everybody makes their own signs, but I bring extras,” Edelsein said amid honking horns while Bob Marley’s “Get Up, Stand Up,” played from the speaker he totes to Cos Cob on Saturdays.

“We feel like we should be here as a conscience – to let our neighbors know, especially our moderate neighbors, know that we are not okay with what’s going on in Washington, DC,” Edelstein said. “We are not okay with the threatened end to democracy. We are not okay with the President acting like a king. We are not okay with the actions of ICE.”

Cos Cob resident, Chris Day, explained his participation. “I can’t just do nothing. I can vote, but I can’t wait until November.”

“Every hour something different that’s crazy comes out, which just waters down all the other crazy, and then everyone just gets used to crazy,” Mr. Day said.

“I don’t want to be out here doing this,” he added. “But that’s how they win.”

Mr. Day, who waived a large American flag, said there were more honks of support than a year ago, which he said was heartening.

But he and Edelstein were particularly unhappy with ICE tactics in Fairfield County.

As Edelstein’s playlist moved on to The Who’s “Won’t Get Fooled Again,” Mr. Day criticized the President.

“He didn’t win the presidential election. He was caught in Florida with the documents. In Georgia tried to fix the vote,” he said. “If he loses ground in November, different versions of the same ridiculousness will be back because he’s given us, virtually every day, doing something illegal. He’s a felon. He’s a rapist.”

A few feet away, Pat Ferris pointed out that the drivers honking weren’t just workers in trucks and vans, but Porsche and BMW drivers beeping and giving the thumbs-up gesture.

“Once it’s near you, it makes a difference,” Ferris said of the ICE activity in Connecticut last week.

“What I notice is I’m not getting any negativity. In the past we were told to shut up. Last week we were called ‘retarded.’ They’ll give us the thumbs down or they’ll root for Trump. But, today it’s amazing. It’s so much beeping and thumbs up.”

As for ICE rounding up immigrants in Connecticut, and the refrain that ICE is only targeting people with criminal records, she exclaimed, “Don’t we all want the criminals gone!”

“It’s just such a cover up. They’re blanketing all immigrants. It’s just evil. Stephen Miller and his quotas, and hiring all these goons. It’s sinful.”

“The mass deportation policy is among all the terrible policies inflicted on the American people,” Edelstein said. “They’re sending them to these camps with terrible conditions, where they are denying people medication and treating them terribly. The conditions are miserable to the point that people are dying. It’s a completely cynical policy. No one in this administration actually believes that these people have anything to do with the downturn of our country. They are not criminals.”

“Statistically, average Americans are much more likely to commit crimes than these so-called felons. These are gardeners, teachers and people who work in kitchens. They are the foundation of America. They are not a threat to society.”

Last week ICE made arrests in Stamford, Bridgeport and Danbury.

“They kidnapped about 100 people,” Edelstein said. “I can guarantee you that almost none of them have any criminal record at all, and many of them have not been accused of, much less convicted of a crime.”

“These are all hard working people. On Monday at Home Depot in Stamford on Main Street, a mother of three kids – one of whom is disabled – was kidnapped in front of her family by ICE. If people think this happens elsewhere or only in Minnesota, they are wrong. This is happening here and now,” Edelstein said.

Edelstein said ICE was rounding up groups of people and using facial recognition software to scan faces.

“If they get a hit, there is absolutely no due process. They are quickly taking people to other states so they have less resources, and to make it harder to get an attorney,” he added.

At a press conference in Danbury on Wednesday, Governor Lamont decried ICE activity in Fairfield County coinciding with the start of the school year.

Approximately 50 members of the Danbury community were detained in the first three days of the week, with the effort starting on the first day of school.

Governor Lamont said people being picked up included those “doing it right” – those participating in the asylum process and those married to US citizens.

The Governor said he was outraged.

“We stand for due process, not the secret police. That’s what this country is about – the fifth and sixth amendment,” Lamont continued. “I was on the phone with Secretary Mullin, and I said, I’m outraged. This is the first day of school…and you have people patrolling around our courthouses and patrolling around schools. Stay away. Let our kids get to school safely.”

Mayor of Danbury, Roberto Alves, who appeared at the press conference with the chief and deputy chief of police, said the Danbury Police Dept does not partner with ICE. He said it was important that the immigrant community knows they can call police if they are victims of crime, victims of domestic abuse, or witness a crime being committed.

text:
Outside a Charlotte Immigration and Customs Enforcement office last fall, a plainclothes officer grabbed William Donovan Stanley from behind and said three words — and they weren’t “you’re under arrest.”

“Come here, motherf—er,” officer Jason Rajabi said as he lunged for the local college student, according to video and testimony revealed in federal court Monday.

Stanley is accused of blocking Rajabi’s car with his body, punching his car window and resisting arrest during a five-person protest outside the south Charlotte immigration office on Tyvola Centre Road on Nov. 16.

His co-defendant — Heather Morrow, a former Mecklenburg county commission candidate — is accused of interfering by parking her Subaru in front of the exit and touching Rajabi’s shoulder as he arrested Stanley.

Morrow and Stanley are on trial in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of North Carolina this week. They each face a misdemeanor charge of assaulting, resisting, opposing, impeding, intimidating and interfering with government officials, as well as petty misdemeanor offenses of: obstructing entrances on a federal property; disrupting government officials’ duties and failing to comply with officials’ orders.

Defense attorneys focused the first day of trial on how immigration officers changed their accounts of what happened overtime and how they interacted with protesters. Federal prosecutors said Morrow and Stanley simply broke the law.

Their case is the last one involving accusations that U.S. citizens assaulted officers during the Trump administration’s “Operation Charlotte’s Web” in November. U.S. Attorney Russ Ferguson’s office dropped charges against others accused of the same. Federal prosecutors also dropped initial federal felony charges filed against Morrow.

They were based on false claims that she jumped on top of Rajabi’s back, her attorneys say.

ICE agents in trial

Video shows Morrow, Stanley and three other people stood in the driveway of the immigration office as Rajabi tried to pull in to start his work day and change into his uniform. Rajabi called for back-up and told the group they would be arrested if they did not move. The protesters followed orders and moved out of the way, bystander video shows. Stanley then ran back in front of Rajabi’s car.

As Rajabi tried to arrest Stanley, Morrow said “stop!” and reached for Rajabi’s shoulder, video shows, before another officer tackled her to the ground.

During the first day of trial Monday, attorney Claire Rauscher (who represents Stanley) asked Rajabi if it was reasonable for a person to try to resist or protect themselves after someone grabbed them from behind and said “come here motherf—er” without identifying themselves.

“Yes, ma’am,” Rajabi, a deployed veteran of the U.S. infantry and ICE officer of six years replied. He added “sir” or “ma’am” to the end of everything he said in front of the jury.

Rauscher repeated the officer’s explicit phrase so much that U.S. District Judge Matthew Orso — recently appointed by President Donald Trump — interjected and asked attorneys to refrain from using it as much as possible.

During cross-examination, attorney Rob Heroy (who represents Morrow) asked why Rajabi’s initial November report says Morrow jumped on his back and that his colleagues quickly detained her from “further assaulting me.” Rajabi testified that Morrow in fact did not affect his attempt to arrest Stanley and did not jump on his back.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Caryn Finley argued that Stanley and Morrow came to federal property, blocked the entrance and exit and refused to follow rules meant to create peacefulness and predictability.

They “escalated the situation to a dangerous point” and had objects of obstruction: cones, cars and themselves. She told jurors to “pay attention to who acts and who reacts.”

Officers, she said, were just doing their jobs.

Heroy told jurors “it was a peaceful protest.”

“Then—”

He paused and slammed his hand down and repeated the phrase of focus:“‘Come here motherf—er.’”

Jurors and gallery members straightened in their seats as he foreshadowed what video and officer testimony would show.

Heroy told the jury of 10 women and four men that they don’t have to believe immigration agents, their government — or even the defense attorneys. But they should pay attention to who they think is reliable narrator in the case.

If convicted, Morrow and Stanley each face up to a year in prison or a $100,000 fine for the misdemeanor charge and one month or $5,000 fines for each of the petty charges.

Tossed ICE assault charges

John Parke Davis and Melissa Owen, attorneys who represented two other men charged with assaulting agents, were in the gallery Monday.

Davis represented Miguel Angel Garcia Martinez, who was accused of using his car as a deadly weapon and hitting agents car during the same week in November when Morrow and Stanley were at the ICE office. iPhone video taken by agents and played in court showed agents planned to “smash” into Martinez.

His charges were dropped soon after.

Owen represented Cristobal Maltos, who was accused of interfering with agents and following them on his way to deliver groceries. Emergency audio showed Maltos called 911 after he said agents sideswiped his car and kept driving. He followed as an operator listened. Agents at a stop light blocked him in, smashed his window and threatened to shoot him.

His charges were thrown out before evidence could be presented in court.

title: The Supreme Court Keeps Finding Reasons to Give Trump What He Wants
description:
In an unsigned 5-4 opinion published on Monday, though, the Supreme Court decided that a president’s unilateral decision to bulldoze part of the White House was totally fine.
As a result, if a federal court eventually rules on the merits that, no, Trump can’t build the ballroom, that conclusion will be academic.
This case started back in December, when the National Trust for Historic Preservation filed a lawsuit arguing that an array of federal statutes prohibit the ballroom’s construction.
Until Trump beat the Trust in court or Congress authorized the ballroom, though, that portion of the project would have to wait.
“The President of the United States is the steward of the White House for future generations of First Families,” Leon wrote.
text:
Last fall, President Donald Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House so that he could build a gigantic honking ballroom in its place, using a conspicuously fuzzy combination of private donations and hundreds of millions of dollars in taxpayer funds that lawmakers very much did not appropriate for that purpose. Federal law prohibits the construction of any new buildings on federal property in Washington, D.C., without the “express authority” of Congress, which, in news I am sure will astonish you, Trump did not bother obtaining first.

In an unsigned 5-4 opinion published on Monday, though, the Supreme Court decided that a president’s unilateral decision to bulldoze part of the White House was totally fine. The justices in the majority strained to avoid saying as much; in the final paragraph of their opinion, they expressly stated that it does not “pass upon the legality of the government’s East Wing project.”

But the upshot of National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation is that whether or not Trump’s already-in-progress ballroom is “legal”—something that, in my view, the Supreme Court of the United States really ought to weigh, but whatever—no one has the power to stop its construction, even temporarily. As a result, if a federal court eventually rules on the merits that, no, Trump can’t build the ballroom, that conclusion will be academic. The ballroom will already be complete, and Getty Images will be awash in photos of Justice Clarence Thomas attending the ribbon-cutting ceremony, cocktail in hand, having an absolute blast.

This case started back in December, when the National Trust for Historic Preservation filed a lawsuit arguing that an array of federal statutes prohibit the ballroom’s construction. To show that it had standing—the legal right to sue—the Trust provided a declaration from Alison K. Hoagland, a history professor who sits on the organization’s board of trustees. In it, Hoagland explained that along with many others, she would “suffer both professional and personal injuries, including to my aesthetic, cultural and historical interests, if a ballroom of the proposed form and scale were constructed.”

In March, D.C. District Court Judge Richard Leon, an appointee of President George W. Bush, agreed, finding that “no statute comes close to giving the President the authority he claims to have.” Leon then entered a preliminary injunction allowing only construction on a below-ground “military installation”—a protective bunker beneath the planned ballroom—to continue while litigation continued, in light of the bunker’s putative importance to national security. Until Trump beat the Trust in court or Congress authorized the ballroom, though, that portion of the project would have to wait.

“The President of the United States is the steward of the White House for future generations of First Families,” Leon wrote. “He is not, however, the owner!”

Leon stayed his order to allow the Trump administration to appeal, and as anyone who has observed construction activity near the White House of late knows, it never took effect. The Supreme Court’s opinion on Monday ensures that it never will.

The thrust of the majority opinion is that Hoagland and the Trust probably do not have standing to sue over the ballroom, since “mere offense, disagreement, or distaste does not qualify” as the sort of “concrete and particularized injury” necessary to establish standing. The majority also found that Trump would suffer “irreparable harm” if he were not allowed to build the ballroom right now, based on the sworn declarations of various Trump gremlins who solemnly attested that their boss’s vanity pet project is very, very important, and that each passing day that he can’t complete it is both a national security risk and a grave injustice.

In a dissent joined by the three liberals, Chief Justice John Roberts argued that under Supreme Court precedent, the Trust has shown that it has standing. As a “historical preservationist,” Roberts argued, Hoagland “can be aesthetically injured in a concrete, particularized way by the transformation of a historic building that she frequently enjoys.” By barring the Trust from suing, he concluded, the majority was allowing “the Executive’s likely infringement of the Legislature’s power of the purse…to continue.”

This is of course right. But the problem with the dissent is that it accepts the majority’s framing—that technically, the case is not about whether Trump can tear down part of the White House to build the Altria Coinbase Palantir Technologies Ballroom Presented By Truth Social, which is a real thing happening in the real world right now. Instead, the dissent is as focused as the majority on parsing standing doctrine, as outlined by the Court in (among other cases) Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife and Spokeo v. Robins in 1992 and 2016, respectively. Throughout, both the majority and the dissenting opinions carefully characterize the ballroom as an initiative of the “federal government,” as if the fact that the subject matter is a flagrantly illegal stunt initiated by a president famous for not giving a shit about the law is just a wild coincidence.

National Trust for Historic Preservation is yet another entry in the canon of cases in which the conservative justices, eager to implement their policy agenda yet reluctant to say so explicitly, cobble together some half-assed gibberish to assert that The Law compels their preferred result. An abstract concept like standing doctrine is especially useful in this context, since its contours are flexible enough to allow judges and justices to greenlight lawsuits from parties with whom they sympathize and, as here, to block lawsuits from parties with whom they do not.

The fight over the ballroom lays bare the absurdity of the Court’s strategy of “resolving” Trump-adjacent cases by pretending to do something else. For Trump and the Trust and anyone else who is not a law professor getting ready to teach civil procedure next week, the only thing that matters here is whether the conservative supermajority’s favorite president gets to do what he wants. The answer is yes, at least until the next Democratic president promises to raze the ballroom, at which point the Court will suddenly rediscover its passion for preserving both D.C. landmarks and the separation of powers, and say, You know what, before we start tearing anything down here, we really ought to let the legal process play out.

text:
An Edmonton-born man who spent months in ICE detention is back in Canada, where he is now sharing his story about the conditions and hurdles he faced while detained.

Curtis Wright, 40, who spent most of his life living in the United States, was held by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas for nine months after returning from a business trip to Mexico in November.

Wright said the reason he was detained stems from a misdemeanor drug possession charge from when he was 17 years old.

Wright said he was motivated to fight to remain in the U.S to try to be with his two young sons from a previous marriage, aged 8 and 11, who are in Texas.

Wright said he was returned to Canada in mid-August, and is temporarily staying at his parents’ house in Kelowna, B.C., with his fiancée, Kayla Thomsen, and their two-year-old daughter.

In an interview with Edmonton AM on Monday, Wright detailed the challenges he faced while struggling to remain south of the border.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

What happened when you returned to Texas after a work trip to Mexico?

When I was going through Immigration and Customs, they asked me to go into secondary screening, which isn't uncommon. I've been through that before, but this began pretty differently.

He right away asked me, “Were you charged with misdemeanor possession back in 2004?”

I said “Yes, I was.”

He said, “OK, make a text to one of your family members. Let them know that this is going to be a while because we're going to have to investigate this further.”

Once I did that, they brought me into a back interview room where I was interrogated almost as if I were on trial, like I had done something wrong at that moment.

Then once the interview was over, he said, “As of this moment, you're now being detained. You'll be taken to a federal facility, and you won't have a court date until Dec. 3rd.” And this was on Nov. 6.

From that point, they moved me to a separate room and then from there they shackled me, put the waist chains around me, handcuffed me to my waist, put on ankle shackles, as if I was some kind of murder convict, and had me wait in a cell then took me to the facility.

Has anything like this ever happened to you previous to this encounter?

Never. I've gone in and out of the U.S. probably over 100 times before this happened. I came to Kelowna to visit my parents at their home just this last summer just a few months before this detainment.

I was under the impression that they were focusing on the worst of the worst, like gang members, and people of that nature. I didn't realize that they were going to be detaining me.

What options did they give you about what could happen next?

Really nothing. The guy informed me that because I was being federally detained there's no bond available to me because they marked me as a visiting alien reentering the country.

I was told later that if ICE had grabbed me in the country, I would have been able to get a bond potentially so I could fight my case outside.

But they purposely marked me as a visiting alien so that I couldn't get a bond. And then he said, “You're just going to have to go through the court case.” So that's essentially what I did.

Then that took this whole nine-month process to go through that court case?

They keep pushing your court case back because the whole idea behind it is they want you to give up. They don't want you to fight your case.

They put you in these horrible facilities and treat you very, very poorly, and they continue to push your court cases back. So you think you're going to court and then they say, “No, actually it's going to be in another three weeks. Oh wait, no, it's going to be in another two weeks.” Because they want you to give up and just go home.

How many times did that happen to you where they pushed it?

For my first court date, it happened four times. I was originally scheduled to have it on Dec. 3 but didn't end up having it until Jan. 16.

After about five months, I finally went through the court case process and lost.

You’re supposed to get three dates and your third date is your trial date where a judge renders a decision. But I didn’t even get the opportunity to fight my case. On my second court date, they just said “Order of removal.”

Then I appealed after that and we tried to get a federal release through a writ of habeas corpus. The whole idea behind that was to get out so I could fight outside, and then we'd continue to do continuances and continuances and continuances waiting for the next political regime or hopefully winning my appeal. But I was never given the opportunity to do that.

You were fighting to be released back into Texas. That's where you called home. I understand that's where some of your family is as well?

The main reason that I was fighting to stay in Texas is because I have two sons with a previous wife.

I knew if I went to Canada they wouldn't be able to come with me. At the time I had 50/50 possession, so I got them half the year.

I fought because I wanted to stay in my children's lives as much as I possibly could, so that's why I stayed for nine months until we exhausted every option.

We had Republican senators write in asking for my release. We had Democrat senators write in asking for my release. We had Texas state representatives, even one individual who was on the board of commissions for Texas State prisons and detention centres, he wrote to ICE, the federal courts, the immigration courts. They all did.

Then I fought my case and we tried federal release. We went to the media. I exhausted every option because, to me, it was important to leave with no regrets, knowing that I did everything I could to stay with my boys. And that one day when I have to tell them why Dad had to leave, I can tell them with honesty that, “Your father did everything he possibly could.” But it just didn't work out.

Can you tell us about what you experienced over those nine months in those centres?

It's the hygiene side of it. There's dirt, mould and grime everywhere. Everything's run down. I mean, you're sharing a small bathroom and showers with 100 men. There are a hundred men in the dorms. The food is just abysmal.

But more than that, it’s the officers that are there in place to be security for you. They yell at you. They curse at you. They threaten you. Solitary confinement is always one of their biggest threats, or moving you to different dorms or taking away privileges.

The lights are on 24 hours a day. You're sleeping in a steel bunk bed with no pillow. You're asked to be counted in your bed five times a day, and it's almost like a psychological and emotional beatdown.

Because, as I mentioned before, they want to make things as uncomfortable as they possibly can for you because they want you to give up and just go back to your home country. You feel like you're less than human.

When did you finally decide to be deported to Canada?

I finally made that decision about eight months in, and then it took about another month to get out.

Because my lawyer had informed me that in the federal courts there's an ongoing case right now pertaining to permanent residence and due process, and that the judge that had my habeas corpus for a federal release was waiting on the ruling of that case, and it had already been ongoing for several months.

The lawyer said the case “could go on for two more weeks or it could go on for two more years. So, you could wait another year, year and a half, let’s say, and then the ruling goes against permanent residents. And then you can’t get release on that anyways.”

At that point, I realized it was just the best thing for my family because even though I'm the one locked up in there, my whole family's going through it. I feel like we were all stuck in this terrible, terrible nightmare.

I thought it was important for the whole family that we just kind of move on and find a way to just move forward with our lives the best way we can and accept what is, and so that's what we're doing.

But again, I love Canada and there was no concern about coming back here. It was simply trying to stay there for my sons.

What are your next steps from here?

My career has been in oil and gas and so, being from Edmonton, it's kind of a perfect spot to pick that right back up. Thankfully, my company that I was working for before in Houston, is going to be opening up a Canadian division just for me to run and try to grow here in Canada.

I've had a lot of wonderful people in my corner, including my employer, and they're going to continue to stick by me and most of my family is in Edmonton — all my aunts, uncles, cousins, my brother and his wife and children are there.

text:
In an op-ed published by MSNOW on August 31, 2026, Congressman James Walkinshaw (VA-11) underscores that Trump is closing legal immigration pathways while scaling mass deportation efforts.

Read the op-ed below or online at MSNOW.

“How many more dads have to die?”

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo’s son asked me that question shortly after his 52-year-old father was fatally shot last month by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer.

For decades, Lorenzo worked construction in Texas to provide for his family. Looking into the eyes of Lorenzo’s two grieving sons, I could see the human cost of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda.

Earlier this year, I traveled to Minneapolis, where the community was grieving Renee Good, a U.S. citizen and mother killed by ICE. After I returned to Washington, I said there would be more deaths if the Trump administration continued its aggressive and unaccountable mass deportation policies.

Sadly, I was right.

At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration agents since Trump’s crackdown began. Alex Pretti, a U.S. citizen and Department of Veterans Affairs intensive care nurse, was killed in Minneapolis in January by Border Patrol agents. In July, Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old father of a 3-year-old daughter, was fatally shot during an ICE operation in Biddeford, Maine.

These deaths, hundreds of miles apart, are the foreseeable consequence of immigration enforcement policies that demand arbitrary arrest totals and disregard common sense, constitutional limits and the value of human life.

Worse, the administration is preparing to widen its campaign. Officials are preparing to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourism visas held by people who have sought or are seeking asylum, the Associated Press reported this week. This will be the largest mass revocation of visas in U.S. history.

But Trump’s immigration trap reaches far beyond people seeking asylum. It ensnares families trying to reunite legally, visa holders facing new uncertainties, longtime workers who have built lives and businesses here and U.S. citizens caught in reckless immigration operations.

First, the administration closes legal doors. In January, the State Department paused immigrant visa issuances to applicants from 75 countries. A federal court vacated that policy on Aug. 21. The visa revocation plan now under consideration would take the approach even further.

Federal law allows people seeking protection to apply for asylum regardless of their current immigration status. Claims that do not meet the law should be denied. But an asylum application is not wrong. It is a request for the fair, individualized process our nation’s law requires.

But after legal avenues are blocked, Trump’s mass deportation apparatus closes in.

White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, the architect of Trump’s immigration policy, has publicly said the administration’s target is 3,000 immigration arrests a day. Local law enforcement agencies don’t operate on quotas for good reason. A quota does not consider who someone is or whether they pose a threat. It merely asks how many. By that standard, a father driving his construction crew to a job site counts the same as a violent criminal. So does a man on his way to work in Maine. So does a 5-year-old child. All help meet the arbitrary quota.

Five-year-old Liam Conejo Ramos was caught in that trap. Photos went viral earlier this year when ICE detained Liam, an innocent in a blue bunny hat, with his father despite a pending asylum case and no order directing their removal at the time. Ordering their release, U.S. District Judge Fred Biery wrote that the case grew from an “ill-conceived and incompetently-implemented government pursuit of daily deportation quotas, apparently even if it requires traumatizing children.”

The administration says it is targeting “the worst of the worst.” But the facts tell a different story. The overwhelming majority of individuals detained by ICE have committed no violent crime. In fact, the focus on quotas has caused ICE and other federal law enforcement agencies to relax their focus on public safety, reassigning investigators away from fentanyl and child sex trafficking work.

That’s not what Americans want. Half of Americans say this deportation campaign has gone too far, including nearly one-quarter of the people who voted for Trump in 2024, according to Politico polling conducted Aug. 8-12. Gallup polling in June found that 73% say immigration is a good thing for the country. They want secure borders, rules people can understand, timely decisions and enforcement focused on genuine threats to public safety.

As the only House Democrat serving on both the homeland security and oversight committees, I have watched accountability inside ICE collapse. In a closed-door briefing in July, ICE officials told members of Congress that the agency had received 56 excessive-force complaints since Trump returned to office. Thirty-two were cleared and the rest were still under investigation as of the briefing. One officer had been referred for possible discipline. No officer had actually been disciplined as of that briefing. Think about that: ICE has 22,000 officers, and not one has faced disciplinary action for violating use-of-force policies.

Last year, Republicans approved $170 billion to expand immigration enforcement. In June, they added an additional $70 billion in funding for ICE and Border Patrol through 2029.

Instead of making these agencies come back to Congress each year and answer for their actions and how they use the money, Republicans locked in funding for years. They did it without adding commonsense reforms such as requiring judicial warrants before agents enter homes, mandating body cameras, and seeking independent investigations when someone is hurt or killed.

That was a choice. The Republican majority chose the blank check, and it has refused to work with Democrats on the lifesaving reforms we are still seeking.

Congress can fund border security and still demand accountability from the agencies that carry it out. It should reopen legal doors, replace arbitrary arrest quotas with focused enforcement, and require judicial warrants, body cameras and independent investigations when people are hurt or killed.

text:
U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds is doubling down on Gov. Ron DeSantis’ hard-line immigration policies as he campaigns to succeed him, warning that local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement should be removed from office.

Speaking Saturday at the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new Miami-Dade Republican Party headquarters in Doral, Donalds said he would oust local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal law enforcement — a stance that would uphold DeSantis’ strict immigration approach, which has empowered Florida law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration arrests and led to the now-closed Alligator Alcatraz.

“If you’re a local official and you are not going to cooperate with federal law enforcement, then yes, you need to be removed from office,” he said.

Under DeSantis, Florida has the highest number of arrests under 287(g) agreements, a program that enables local law enforcement and governments to perform certain immigration enforcement activities typically handled by federal authorities.

When local officials have pushed back against signing an agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, James Uthmeier, DeSantis appointed attorney general, has warned that the governor could remove them from office.

Donalds, who has supported President Donald Trump’s crackdown on immigrant communities, said as governor, his administration “will cooperate through 287(g), and we will follow the law.”

“There aren’t going to be sanctuary jurisdictions in Florida,” he said.

The DeSantis administration declared illegal immigration an emergency in the Sunshine State in 2023 and spent more than $1 billion to build and operate Alligator Alcatraz, an immigration detention center in the middle of the Everglades. It closed in June after DeSantis said it had fulfilled its goal of providing temporary, needed space to hold immigrants apprehended by federal immigration officials.

Donalds’ comments come amid ongoing debates in the City of Miami, where immigration advocates have pushed for the city’s Democratic Mayor, Eileen Higgins, and the Miami City Commission to end an agreement partnering local police with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

READ MORE: Miami’s Democratic mayor attacked in ads by immigration-advocacy group

And in Doral, where the nation’s largest Venezuelan-American community is experiencing an increase in immigration raids, Rafael Pineyro, the only Venezuelan-American on the City Council, has pushed back against the immigration crackdown.

Pineyro, a Republican, has called immigration enforcement officials’ focus on not just criminals but also families in the community with pending immigration cases “tragic.”

READ MORE: ‘A tragic moment’: Immigration crackdown intensifies in Doral, home to thousands of Venezuelans

David Jolly, the Democratic candidate for governor, thinks 287(g) agreements should be suspended and that DeSantis’ mandate that local agencies must sign on is a problem.

Jolly said local law enforcement knows how best to keep their communities safe and should not be mandated to these agreements that strip resources away from things like child sex crimes.

“Until we see the reforms, show us your badge, show us your face, show us the judicial warrant. I do think [the agreements] should be suspended,” Jolly said at his primary election night watch party in Miami Lakes. “Once those reforms are in place, I trust local law enforcement.”

Immigration is a key concern in South Florida, as hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Venezuelans have lost their Temporary Protected Status, a humanitarian program that allowed them to work and prevented deportation.

Donalds told reporters Saturday that the humanitarian program was meant to be temporary. He blamed Democrats for the fallout, saying “they took a temporary program and made it permanent,” though a House bill to extend TPS for Haitians that passed in April included the support of 10 Republicans, including Miami’s Mario Diaz-Balart, Carlos Gimenez and Maria Elvira Salazar.

When asked by reporters what his message was to the Venezuelan-American voters who feel their lives were upended by immigration raids, Donalds said, “if you’re Venezuelan and you’re here on TPS, Temporary Protected Status, it has always been a temporary program. That’s number one.”

“Number two, the president of the United States and Secretary of State Marco Rubio did the right thing by getting rid of the Maduro regime, which was, frankly, a narco-terrorist regime that was actually destroying the way of life and the safety in Venezuela.”

Some of Donalds’ Republican colleagues in Congress believe that the Trump administration’s strict approach to immigration could have some negative effects for Republicans in the upcoming November elections.

Salazar, who is up for reelection, has become a critic of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, which has seen Cubans deported to Mexico and to countries in Africa.

Salazar has remained a supporter of Trump, but has warned the administration that its immigration approach might cost the Republicans the midterm elections.

When Mexico receives third-country deportees at the U.S. border, its authorities swiftly board them onto buses and transport them to the same southern-border cities.
Once they arrive in Tapachula, deported people—Mexican and third-country alike—form a scared, traumatized, destitute, vulnerable, and invisible population.

text:
Team WOLA

Report in English [PDF] – Report in Spanish [PDF]

This release as a PDF – Este comunicado en español (PDF)

Podcast audio in Spanish – Podcast video with English subtitles

Tapachula, Nogales, and Washington, August 31, 2026: The Trump administration’s “mass deportations” are generating a full-blown humanitarian crisis at Mexico’s northern and southern border regions, according to a new brief from three U.S. and Mexican organizations. Banished to the South: The Human Cost of Deportation combines work by the Fray Matías de Córdova Center for Human Rights in Tapachula, Mexico, near the Guatemalan border; the Kino Border Initiative at the U.S.-Mexico border in Nogales, Arizona and Sonora; and the Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA), in Washington, DC. Among the groups’ alarming findings:

Unlike in past years, when most people whom the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) was deporting into Mexico were recent border crossers, the deported population is now made up mostly of people arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in the U.S. interior, usually after spending years or decades living in the United States.

Over 1,100 deported people per month in Mexico are citizens of other Latin American nations, with a large number from Cuba and Venezuela.

Many of the Mexican or third-country nationals being deported had been living in the United States with a status—humanitarian parole, Temporary Protected Status, or pending asylum applications—that the Trump administration has since terminated or revoked.

Since mid-April, ICE has rarely deported Mexican citizens across the 1,954-mile land border. Instead, and at significant expense, the agency is flying them to cities in Mexico’s interior, usually the southern border-zone cities of Villahermosa, Tabasco and Tapachula, Chiapas.

When Mexico receives third-country deportees at the U.S. border, its authorities swiftly board them onto buses and transport them to the same southern-border cities.

Once they arrive in Tapachula, deported people—Mexican and third-country alike—form a scared, traumatized, destitute, vulnerable, and invisible population. Mexico’s government gives third-country citizens just ten days to remain in the country, with its overstretched asylum system the only option for most.

ICE routinely fails to return people’s identity documents, making it hard to prove their citizenship, apply for protection, or even receive electronic money transfers. Those who wish to risk return to countries of origin cannot do so without their confiscated documents.

Many people encountered in Nogales and Tapachula say that ICE separated them from their U.S. citizen children and did not give them an opportunity to choose to be deported with them.

Trapped in Tapachula, third-country migrants are subject to a “revolving door” of detention and release, unable to work legally or to leave Mexico’s southernmost state. Along with recently deported Mexican citizens, they are vulnerable to organized crime groups that prey on them: ransom kidnappings are a constant risk.

This ever-worsening situation is not inevitable: it is the result of policy choices, the three organizations contend. Washington’s severe anti-immigrant policies bear most of the blame. But Mexico City is also failing to do much within its power to ease the trauma.

The mass deportations must stop, and the United States needs to restore due process to protection-seeking migrants immediately. Until that happens, Banished to the South offers a series of common-sense recommendations for steps that Mexico’s state can take to support the deported people it is receiving: both its own citizens and those from other countries.

More articles

text:
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy appeared on national television on Aug. 28 to discuss the presence of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Connecticut. Over the course of a week, the agency made about 100 reported arrests, according to activists, but ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have provided limited details and not confirmed a total.

Murphy, in his appearance on MS NOW’s 'Morning Joe' show, spoke about an incident involving family members being detained by ICE at a bus stop shortly after children got on. The story had been relayed to Murphy and other public officials during the week through activists who were involved in determining just how many people were being arrested and connecting them to lawyers and family members. In Murphy’s case, he said he got a call from Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“After the kids had boarded the school buses, they were taking the parents into custody,” Murphy said.

The incident, however, is disputed by DHS. They say they did arrest a 28-year-old Ecuadorian man in Danbury on Wednesday, Aug. 26, but said he was alone in his vehicle and nowhere near a bus stop.

“Any claim that ICE targeted parents at a school bus stop is false,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to CT Insider.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

While there were many incidents throughout the week captured on video, this is an incident that has not been widely surfaced — largely only talked about. Because ICE does not release information on every arrest, it's unclear what exactly happened. What is clear is that DHS and supporters in Danbury remain far apart on details while it continues to be talked about.

Carolina Bortolleto of Danbury United for Immigrants said Monday that she could not provide details about the individual people involved, but said the group had spoken to people in the neighborhood who witnessed ICE activity around a bus stop. Bortolleto said children also saw federal agents around the bus stop, and that the arrests have spread fear well beyond the families directly involved.

“We’ve spoken with community members that kids just in Danbury generally are very scared,” she said. Parents, she said, are afraid “to walk the kids to school, to take the kids to the bus stop.”

The dispute reached the White House’s top immigration official Sunday, when CNN reporter Dana Bash asked border czar Tom Homan on 'State of the Union' whether a school bus stop was a place where parents could be arrested.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Homan said the Trump administration had eliminated the previous restrictions governing immigration enforcement in certain sensitive locations, but said agents had not been making arrests inside elementary schools, hospitals or churches. As for the Danbury allegation, Homan said he did not know whether it had happened.

“Did somebody arrest somebody at a bus stop? I’m not aware of that,” Homan said.

Asked specifically about the Connecticut incident — and told that Murphy, Gov. Ned Lamont and Alves had said it happened — Homan said he would check.

“I’ll make an inquiry to Department of Homeland Security,” he said.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Murphy countered in a statement to CT Insider Monday.

“Trump's Border Czar didn't deny ICE targeted school bus stops in Danbury, even when asked directly," Murphy said. "A person was hospitalized, children are living in fear, and workers are afraid to show up to work while this administration dodges questions about their terror campaign in Danbury.”

The department said ICE agents were carrying out a “targeted operation” Wednesday when they stopped Leonel Geovanny Morocho-Arteaga, 28, of Ecuador. He has not been able to be reached for comment.

“The vehicle stop did not take place in the vicinity of a bus stop, and Morocho-Arteaga was alone,” the spokesperson said.

DHS said Morocho-Arteaga entered the United States illegally and was arrested by U.S. Customs and Border Protection in July 2021 before being released into the country. Agents found a large kitchen knife in the center console during Wednesday’s arrest, according to the department.

DHS also said a child connected to the case was with her mother, saying that “the child is under the guardianship of her mother.” The department did not explain the child’s relationship to Morocho-Arteaga or why it included that information in its response.

Nor did the statement make clear whether Morocho-Arteaga was the person involved in the bus-stop incident described by Murphy, Lamont and local advocates, or whether DHS was addressing a separate arrest made during the same wave of enforcement.

There has also been dispute over what day the bus stop arrest might have happened.

Danbury Unites for Immigrants said it had confirmed 94 arrests across Connecticut during the week, including 64 in Danbury. ICE has not confirmed the group’s overall count or released a comprehensive list of the people arrested.

Agents were also reported making arrests in Stamford and other Connecticut communities, while much of the most visible activity centered on Danbury. Videos from the city showed federal agents arresting day laborers in Kennedy Park, struggling with men in the street and detaining a man outside a preschool. text:
The Trump administration plans to purchase robot dogs made by a Massachusetts company for its immigration enforcement operations.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement wants to spend up to $2 million on robots from Boston Dynamics, according to a funding document from the Department of Homeland Security.

The robot known as "Spot" is one of Boston Dynamics' most recognized products. It's a dog-like machine with four legs, and equipped with cameras and sensors that can detect things like hazardous gas. It can also climb stairs and navigate through rough terrain.

The technology would provide ICE with the capability to remotely operate the robots "for inspection, situational awareness, and hazard assessment in environments that may pose risks to personnel," according to the DHS document.

ICE said the robot gives them an additional safety tool and doesn't replace law enforcement officers or human judgement.

"Like with our other law enforcement partners around the country, this robot platform provides law enforcement officers with an additional tool to safely assess potentially dangerous situations before placing personnel or the public at risk," an ICE spokesperson said in a statement. "It can provide real-time situational awareness in hazardous, confined, or tactically uncertain environments, allowing officers to make more informed decisions and, when possible, resolve incidents without immediately introducing personnel into a dangerous area."

Boston Dynamics said it sells its robot to many government agencies and public safety organizations. The robots have typically been used after natural disasters, in search and rescue operations, and to inspect suspicious packages, among other things, according to the company.

"The robots are used to keep people out of harm’s way and aid first responders in assessing dangerous situations," the company said in a statement.

The Trump administration's immigration crackdown has drawn criticism of its tactics and concerns about civil rights after several fatal ICE shootings and clashes with protesters. Several cities in the state have moved to restrict ICE operations, and Gov. Maura Healey recently signed a law to protect people from warrantless arrests.

Boston Dynamics said "any attempted weaponization of Boston Dynamics’ robots is strictly prohibited" under its terms and conditions. The terms say those who purchase their product must agree to their ethical principles, which state the company "will not authorize nor partner with those who wish to use our robots as weapons or autonomous targeting systems."

"If our products are being used for harm, we will take appropriate measures to mitigate that misuse," the page read.

It's unclear what those mitigation measures would be. Boston Dynamics did not respond to questions about what happens if their terms and conditions or ethical principles are violated.

An open letter spearheaded by Boston Dynamics to the robotics community about weaponization said "when possible, we will carefully review our customers’ intended applications to avoid potential weaponization." The letter also called on policymakers to help promote the safe use of robots and prohibit their misuse.

According to those Boston Dynamics terms, U.S. public safety and law enforcement users must agree to have a policy on how Spot is used and make it public before using the technology.

The company has said it would "not authorize nor partner" with those who do not comply with privacy and civil rights laws.

description:

The newly proposed H-1B fee would not, however, apply to extension, change of employer, or cap-exempt petitions.
Following the July 2026 appellate court order, USCIS is not permitted to collect the fee announced in September 2025.
Notably, unlike the prior $100,000 fee imposed through last fall’s presidential proclamation, this proposal will proceed through formal notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).

text:
On the heels of the decision of the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit to deny the U.S. government’s appeal designed to implement the September 2025 $100,000 H-1B visa fee, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security has proposed an additional H-1B visa fee of $103,265. The newly proposed fee would apply to all cap-subject H-1B petitions, including those eligible for the advanced degree exemption, resulting in a more expansive application than the prior six-figure fee. The newly proposed H-1B fee would not, however, apply to extension, change of employer, or cap-exempt petitions.

In addition, major U.S. media outlets have reported that the executive branch is considering a proposal to add a $100,000 fee to OPT, a common program through which international students contribute to U.S. companies for up to three years after graduation from a U.S. academic institution.

These announcements from USCIS and the executive branch come nearly one year after the release of the proclamation titled “Restriction on Entry of Certain Nonimmigrant Workers.” Under the proclamation, certain H-1B petitions must be accompanied by an additional $100,000 payment as a condition of eligibility. As drafted and clarified, the proclamation does not apply to petitions requesting an amendment, change of status, or extension of stay for individuals already present in the United States, and only applies if USCIS determines the individual is ineligible for a change of status, amendment, or extension of stay. However, the original six-figure fee has faced a significant scrutiny, delaying its complete and consistent implementation. Following the July 2026 appellate court order, USCIS is not permitted to collect the fee announced in September 2025.

In contrast, the newly proposed H-1B visa fee of $103,265 would apply to all cap-subject petitions following the completion of a public comment period set to end on Sept. 24. Notably, unlike the prior $100,000 fee imposed through last fall’s presidential proclamation, this proposal will proceed through formal notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). After completion of the notice-and-comment process, USCIS will announce whether it will proceed with its implementation, creating a far more expansive group of H-1B applicants subject to the six-figure fee.

Turning to the published rationale, USCIS has stated that, if implemented, the newly proposed H-1B visa fee would generate the revenue needed to cover costs associated with administering a lawful immigration system, such as the adjudication of immigration benefits, fraud detection and national security vetting, systems modernization, records and fee collection operations, immigration court operations, consular visa processing, labor standards enforcement, and interagency coordination. According to current estimates released by USCIS, the proposed fee program would generate approximately $8.8 billion annually. The OPT fee would also create a significant revenue source, estimated to exceed $40 billion should all 400,000 international graduates pay the fee in order to work in the U.S. following graduation.

The Democrats sent their letter days after ICE granted a $16.7 million no-bid contract to the Kentucky-based firm Compliant Technologies for 6,000 pairs of electric shock gloves, ignoring the protests of lawmakers and human rights groups.
The ACLU, Physicians for Human Rights, and the Center for Victims of Torture (CVT) are among the advocacy organizations that have decried ICE plans to equip its agents with the gloves.

text:
A group of House Democrats on Monday demanded the immediate cancellation of a nearly $17 million federal contract to provide electric shock gloves to Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, who have been unleashed on American cities under the second Trump administration and enabled to commit horrific—and, in some cases, deadly—abuses against undocumented immigrants and American citizens.

The Democratic lawmakers, led by Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois, expressed "profound alarm" over the contract in a new letter to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose agency oversees ICE. The letter's 50 signatories wrote that the devices, known as Generated Low Output Voltage Emitters (GLOVE), are "designed to inflict severe pain without leaving physical evidence or visible optics," making them "a uniquely dangerous tool for unaccountable abuse."

"We demand the immediate cancellation of this contract and a total ban on the deployment of these abusive devices across all immigration enforcement and detention operations," the lawmakers continued. "The rollout of these weapons to thousands of field agents across ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations and Homeland Security Investigations contributes to a DHS environment already under widespread scrutiny for state-sanctioned abuse, torture, and arbitrary cruelty."

The Democrats sent their letter days after ICE granted a $16.7 million no-bid contract to the Kentucky-based firm Compliant Technologies for 6,000 pairs of electric shock gloves, ignoring the protests of lawmakers and human rights groups.

The ACLU, Physicians for Human Rights, and the Center for Victims of Torture (CVT) are among the advocacy organizations that have decried ICE plans to equip its agents with the gloves. CVT has described the devices as "inherently abusive equipment that facilitates torture."

In their Monday letter, the group of House Democrats warned that the "dangers of these 'less-lethal' weapons are not theoretical," pointing to the case of a 43-year-old man in Kentucky who died after corrections officers shocked him dozens of times with electric gloves.

More than 50 people have died in ICE custody during President Donald Trump's second term.

"This administration continues to outfit ICE and [Customs and Border Protection] with the tools of an occupying paramilitary force—despite widespread human rights violations carried out by its agents during immigration enforcement actions," the lawmakers wrote. "Introducing low-visibility electric shock weapons into our immigration enforcement system is an unacceptable escalation that prioritizes physical intimidation and unaccountable force over human safety and administrative accountability.

On top of calling for cancellation of the contract, the House Democrats demanded information on any threat assessments ICE conducted before awarding the contract, whether the agency has trained its officers with electric shock gloves, and whether DHS intends to implement any productions to "prevent officers from using them for punitive measures, retaliation, or against non-threatening individuals."

"We reiterate our demand that you immediately halt the acquisition and deployment of electric shock gloves, cancel the contract, and refocus the Department’s resources on accountability and humanitarian standards rather than expanding a paramilitary apparatus," the lawmakers wrote.

text:
Federal immigration authorities conducted a large-scale enforcement operation in Memphis early Sunday that immigrant advocacy groups say resulted in the detention of more than 100 people at a local bar.

The operation took place around 1 a.m. at El Corralón, a business on Macon Road in the city's Berclair neighborhood, advocates said. A spokesperson for the advocacy organization Vecindarios901 told Newsweek that federal agents detained more than 100 people and transported them from the scene on buses. The figure has not been independently verified by authorities.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement confirmed that it carried out what it described as a "multi-agency targeted enforcement operation" in Memphis on August 30 but released few details, citing an ongoing investigation.

Read More on News

"More information will be released when available," an ICE spokesperson told Memphis Commercial Appeal.

The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation told Newsweek it executed search warrants Sunday morning at a business in the 3000 block of Macon Road as part of an ongoing investigation.

Vecindarios901 has said it believes the operation was the largest immigration raid in Memphis history.

DHS, the Memphis Police Department, the Tennessee Highway Patrol, Mayor Paul Young's office, and the Shelby County Sheriff's Office have been contacted for comment.

According to Vecindarios901, agents arrived with a search warrant related to an investigation involving alleged illegal gambling machines and possible drug activity at the establishment. The group said individuals who were inside the business at the time were detained during the operation.

Memphis Mayor Paul Young said in a statement on August 30 that the operation was "unsettling" for community members.

Mayor Young added that the Memphis Police Department was not involved in planning or conducting the federal action. According to Young and the department, city officers responded only after federal agencies requested assistance with traffic and crowd control as people gathered in the area. MPD said its officers did not arrest or detain anyone.

“I know that distinction does not erase the fear people are feeling today. There are questions we do not yet have answers to, particularly about actions taken by federal authorities. But I can assure you of this: the people impacted by what happened this morning are our neighbors. They are part of our Memphis community, and they deserve to be treated with dignity,” he said.

Memphis Police Department (MPD) said officers were called to Macon Road near Maria Street around 3:15 a.m. to provide traffic and crowd control during an operation conducted by HSI and ICE, according to Action News 5.

MPD added it was not involved in planning or executing the operation and that its officers did not make any arrests or detentions.

“To see the kids get in the middle of the street, crying for their parents, saying ‘Mom, Dad, let them go. That’s the only thing that I have.’ That was really, really breaking my heart,” Reina Avina, a witness, told Action News 5.

The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition said the operation resulted in "community members detained and taken away on buses, with little information as to why and where they were being taken."

“When more than 100 people are violently rounded up in the middle of the night it sends devastating shockwaves through the entire community," Lisa Sherman Luna, Executive Director at The Tennessee Immigrant and Refugee Rights Coalition, said in a statement shared with Newsweek.

A spokesperson for the Memphis Safe Task Force told Memphis Commercial Appeal that the operation was not conducted by the task force.

Meanwhile, a coalition of Memphis businesses opposed to immigration enforcement operations said more than 50 local establishments have pledged to refuse service to members of the Memphis Safe Task Force, a multi-agency crime initiative operating in the city. Organizers with the "Free the 901" campaign said 48 businesses have publicly joined the effort, with others participating privately, and released a letter calling on elected officials to end the task force's presence in Memphis.

Questions about the scope of the operation and the status of those detained remained unresolved on Monday. Authorities have not publicly released the number of people taken into custody, their identities, where they were transported, or whether any criminal charges have been filed.

A protest was held at the AutoZone on 4394 Summer Avenue on Sunday following the raid. Protesters gathered near the AutoZone on Summer Avenue to voice their opposition to the local ICE operation, video shows. Additional footage captures demonstrators lining the sidewalk of Summer Avenue near a local Baptist church, carrying signs.
